Below is a structured, detailed description of the “Input Description” table (Chapter 3 of the HASE manual), highlighting each input record, its purpose, and its role in setting up a half-space soil–structure interaction analysis. This description is intended to guide knowledge-ingestion into a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) vector store.

1.  Input‐Language (Section 3.1, p. 3-1)  
    •  Purpose: Declares which input convention HASE should expect (e.g. SOFiSTiK DYNAM language).  
    •  Key aspects:  
       –  Keyword syntax  
       –  Field delimiters, data formats  
    •  Notes: Always the first record; defaults are inherited from the global static-program settings.

2.  Input‐Records (Section 3.2, p. 3-2)  
    •  Purpose: Lists all subsequent HASE keywords.  
    •  Key aspects:  
       –  Order‐of‐precedence rules  
       –  Conditional activation/deactivation of records  
       –  Inclusion of external files via ECHO commands  
    •  Notes: Acts as the master table of contents for the HASE input deck.

3.  CTRL – Control of the Analysis Method (Section 3.3, p. 3-3)  
    •  Purpose: Selects the type of analysis: static coupling vs. independent settlement.  
    •  Fields include:  
       –  ISTAT (0 = settlement only; 1 = static-structure coupling)  
       –  OPTIO flags for plasticity, damping, iterative solver settings  
    •  Defaults: static coupling enabled, no plasticity.

4.  GRP – Selection of Element Groups (Section 3.4, p. 3-4)  
    •  Purpose: Defines which structural finite‐element groups interface with the half‐space.  
    •  Fields include:  
       –  Group IDs  
       –  Degrees of freedom (translation/rotation) to be coupled  
    •  Notes: Missing GRP record means no coupling → zero soil stiffness.

5.  HALF – Halfspace Definition (Section 3.5, p. 3-5)  
    •  Purpose: Specifies global halfspace parameters.  
    •  Key parameters:  
       –  RINF – maximum influence radius (to sparsify Ksoil)  
       –  NQ / NR – discretization orders in circumferential/radial directions  
       –  ILAY – flag for layered vs. homogeneous halfspace  
    •  Defaults: RINF large (full coupling), coarse discretization.

6.  BORE – Selection of Bore Profiles (Section 3.6, p. 3-6)  
    •  Purpose: Links user‐defined boreholes to soil‐property interpolation schemes.  
    •  Fields include:  
       –  Bore ID, x/y location  
       –  Soil‐layer thicknesses, material IDs  
       –  Interpolation weight parameters (for COOR, QUAD, LAYR)  
    •  Notes: At least one BORE record is mandatory for layered half-space.

7.  PILE – Internal Piles in the Halfspace (Section 3.7, p. 3-7)  
    •  Purpose: Defines piles embedded in the soil (internal HASE piles).  
    •  Fields include:  
       –  Pile axis geometry (start/end nodes)  
       –  Cross‐sectional stiffness, end‐bearing parameters  
    •  Extended Piles (XPIL) are handled via XPILE records (Section 2.8.2).

8.  PLAS – Plasticizing (Section 3.8, p. 3-9)  
    •  Purpose: Activates non-linear (plastic) soil behavior in settlement analyses.  
    •  Fields include:  
       –  Yield‐stress models (Mohr‐Coulomb, Drucker‐Prager)  
       –  Hardening/softening parameters  
    •  Notes: Only valid if CTRL plasticity flag is switched on.

9.  LOAR – Load Radii (Section 3.9, p. 3-11)  
    •  Purpose: Defines rigid bearing areas on which loads are applied.  
    •  Fields include:  
       –  LOAR_ID, radius, vertical offset  
       –  Load‐distribution type (uniform, triangular)  
    •  Notes: Used internally by subsequent LOAD records.

10.  LC – Load Case (Section 3.10, p. 3-12)  
    •  Purpose: Groups individual loads into named load cases.  
    •  Fields include:  
       –  LC_ID, description  
       –  Combination coefficients for superposition  
    •  Defaults: One load case if no LC record is present.

11.  LOAD – Single Loads (Section 3.11, p. 3-14)  
    •  Purpose: Applies point, line, or area loads to the half-space interface.  
    •  Fields include:  
       –  LOAD_ID, LC_ID reference  
       –  Node or LOAR_ID, force components, load type (static, line)  
    •  Notes: Multiple LOAD records can reference the same load case.

12.  SELE – Results Selection (Section 3.12, p. 3-15)  
    •  Purpose: Chooses which results (displacements, stresses, settlements) are output.  
    •  Fields include:  
       –  Result types (UX, UZ, TXZ, normal stress)  
       –  Node/element selection lists  
    •  Defaults: Displacements in all DOF at coupling nodes.

13.  SELP – Selection of the Plot Representation (Section 3.13, p. 3-16)  
    •  Purpose: Configures graphical output: contour plots, vector fields.  
    •  Fields include:  
       –  Plot type (contour, isoline, vector)  
       –  Color scales, contour intervals, view angles  
    •  Notes: Works in conjunction with the SOFiSTiK post‐processor.

14.  ECHO – Output Control (Section 3.14, p. 3-19)  
    •  Purpose: Controls the verbosity of the input echo and result listings.  
    •  Flags include:  
       –  Echo on/off for each keyword group  
       –  Detail levels for diagnostic printouts  
    •  Default: Echo all major records, suppress minor intermediate tables.

This structured breakdown captures each input record’s function within HASE and maps it to its manual location, allowing a RAG pipeline to retrieve both semantic role and exact page reference when answering user queries.

The input “table” is in fact a fragment of the manual’s contents, organized as a three-column listing: a section number, a title, and the starting page.  Below is a detailed breakdown of its structure and contents:

3. Chapter 1: Task Description (Page 1-1)  
   • A standalone entry “1 Task Description.”  
   • Begins on page labeled “1-1,” following the manual’s mixed decimal pagination for chapters.

4. Chapter 4: Input Data Checklists (Page 4-1 onward)  
   • Main heading: “4 Check List for Bore Profiles” – page 4-1  
   • Subsections (all start at page 4-1 unless otherwise noted):

   • This chapter gathers all pre-processing checks the user must perform: defining borehole profiles, assigning soil parameters to structure-interface nodes, specifying the half-space (layered soil) properties, pile definitions, and validation of node and load data. The rapid page-turn (4-1 to 4-3) signals concise checklists rather than lengthy narrative.

5. Chapter 5: Examples (Page 5-1 onward)  
   • Heading “Examples” followed by individual numbered case studies:  
     5.1 Base Plate Calculated with Stiffness Coefficient Method – page 5-2  
     5.2 Constant Soil Profile – Three-dimensional Frame with a Plate – page 5-7  
     5.3 Interpolation with Weight Factor – page 5-12  
     5.4 Stresses in the Halfspace – page 5-16  
     5.5 Pile-Slab Foundation with Extended Piles – page 5-18  
   • These five examples illustrate progressively more complex uses of HASE, from basic plate stiffness to 3D frames, advanced interpolation schemes, stress/post-processing, and combined pile-slab systems.

6. Bibliography (Page 5-21)  
   • Listed after the examples, indicating source references, standards, and further reading.

7. Contextual Notes (from the surrounding text)  
   • The manual describes HASE (Half-Space Analysis for Static Soil-Structure Interaction), part of the SOFiSTiK suite (Service Pack 2025-4).  
   • HASE uses semi-analytical half-space theory to generate a soil stiffness matrix, which is then linked in module ASE for static analysis.  
   • Users can define layered, radially varying soil profiles via four interpolation schemes: CONS, QUAD, COOR, LAYR.  
   • The basic version handles plane slabs; the expanded version supports full 3D soil domains.

 1 Task Description
 One of the ways to model the static soil-structure interaction is to model the soil according to the Winkler assumption. This method is relatively simple to use but cannot take into consideration the shear deformations within the soil.
 One of the most accurate methods is to model the soil using 3D finite elements. This however requires a huge number of soil elements which in many cases can sever times exceed the number of elements needed for modeling of the structure itself, which is usually the main part of interest for structural engineers.
 In HASE module a sub-structuring technique, in which the structure will be represented using standard finite elements, while the soil will be modeled semi-analytically using the half-space theory, is adopted. The connection between the two substructures will be assured by stiff- ness/flexibility coefficients at the soil-structure interface nodes. This method overcomes the problems of the other two techniques. It takes into consideration the shear deformations within the soil and it does not require explicit discreet modeling of the entire soil domain.
 Based on the halfspace theory, module HASE calculates the stiffness matrix representing the soil part of the static soil-structure interaction system. The soil- structure interaction analysis itself is then preformed in module ASE, in which the soil stiffness matrix is linked with the structure part and the response of the entire system under the prescribed loads is calculated.
 Once the static analysis is finished, HASE can be used for post-processing to determine stresses and settlements of the half-space (soil) due to the supporting forces calculated in the static analysis. It is also possible to perform independent settlement analysis within HASE, where the loads are directly applied to the half- space.

Once the static analysis is finished, HASE can be used for post-processing to determine stresses and settlements of the half-space (soil) due to the supporting forces calculated in the static analysis. It is also possible to perform independent settlement analysis within HASE, where the loads are directly applied to the half- space..
 It is possible to define layered half-space with soil parameters and layer thickness varying in vertical as well as in the radial direction. Therefore each point at the soil-structure inter- face can have different soil-parameters associated to it. This is achieved by interpolating the soil-properties and layer thicknesses from the defined bore profiles. There are following inter- polation schemes available:
 1. CONS - Constant soil profile at all the points of the half-space
 2. QUAD - Bilinear interpolation of a separate system containing a discretised model of the soil
 3. COOR - Interpolation of bore profiles using weight functions
 4. LAYR - Interpolation of the soil properties from the 3D triangular prism mesh model of the layered half-space defined by the bore profile distribution on the half-space surface
 The stiffness matrix does not need to be full in order to be processed. Therefore, the influence of points which are far away from each other (i.e., their distance is above a predefined limit) can be ignored to reduce CPU time.
 In the basic version of HASE, the program processes halfspace problems for plane slab struc- tures. The halfspace for three-dimensional systems is only available in the expanded version.

The program HASE first determines the flexibility matrix. This describes the displacement of a point due to a force on the point k within the half-space. The inverse of the flexibility matrix is the stiffness matrix. The entire calculation consists of five main parts (Bellmann and Radmanovi´c [1]):
 1. Calculation of the soil-profile distribution in the plan view
 2. Calculation of the flexibility matrix
 Inversion and storage of the stiffness matrix
 4. Static calculation including structural elements
 5. Determination of the stresses in the soil due to the calculated displacements.
 The steps 1,2,3 and 5 are executed by HASE. The third step is the most costly in terms of CPU time, accounting for up to 90% of the entire CPU time. However, for a given system, Step 3 need only be calculated once.
 For a half-space analysis with a small or sparse stiffness matrix, Step 3 does not necessarily have to be performed by HASE.
 Requirements:
 analysis of each loadcase separately in ASE with SYST PROB NONL and STEX NONL 1
 •
 Then ASE has to iteratively obtain stiffnesses from the half-space, but it can use the sparse solver much more efficiently and is therefore much faster for certain large systems. In this case, the inversion of the flexibility matrix in HASE can be switched off with CTRL SOLV NONL, because the flexibility matrix is not used. For an example, see hase2.dat.
 A previously generated half-space matrix can simply be reused after a modification to the system. A new calculation of the stiffness matrix is only necessary if the coordinates or the numbering of the contact nodes to the half-space have been changed.

The soil bore profiles position and inclinations are defined in AQUA with the record BORE. Stiffness and resistance soil properties as well as the layer disposition along the bore profile axis are defined using BLAY record. The start depth of the first layer of the bore profile should be on the surface of the half-space (record HALF item Z). If the half-space surface is below the start depth of a bore profile a warning message will appear. If the half-space surface is above the start depth of a bore profile an error message will appear.

The image is presented in two adjacent panels, labeled “a)” on the left and “b)” on the right. Together they illustrate the LAYR interpolation method used to map layered soil properties from a set of bore‐profile locations into a continuous half‐space model.

Panel a) – Surface Triangulation of Bore Profiles  
• Red circular markers represent the horizontal positions of individual bore profiles on the soil‐structure interface (the half‐space surface).  
• Black straight lines connect these markers, forming a network of non‐overlapping triangles (a Delaunay‐style triangulation) that spans the convex hull of all bore points.  
• One central marker is annotated “BP” by a small arrow, indicating an example bore‐profile node from which a vertical soil column will be extruded in the next step.  
• The irregular planimetry of the triangles shows how any arbitrary distribution of bore locations (minimum three points forming a convex polygon) can be meshed without requiring a secondary Cartesian grid.  

Panel b) – 3D Extruded Triangular Prisms with Layered Soil  
• The triangular surface mesh from panel a) has been extruded downward along each bore‐profile axis to build a three‐dimensional tessellation of triangular‐prism elements.  
• Internally, each prism is divided into three vertical layers of differing thickness, corresponding to three distinct strata encountered in the bore logs. These layers are visualized by discrete color bands:  
  – The uppermost layer is rendered in bright orange  
  – The intermediate layer in yellow  
  – The lowermost layer in dark red/brown tones  
• The prisms’ side faces take the color of the layer they belong to, so that vertical variation in soil‐property thickness is clearly visible on all faces of the extruded block.  
• A small triad of colored arrows in one corner denotes the global coordinate axes:  
  – Red for the X‐direction  
  – Green for the Y‐direction  
  – Blue for the vertical Z‐direction  
• Although the prisms geometrically define discrete subdomains carrying exact bore‐profile parameters at their corner nodes, they are used purely for interpolation of soil stiffness, shear strength, unit weight and other properties. The structural analysis itself relies on half‐space theory rather than a solid‐element stiffness matrix.  

Overall, the figure demonstrates how method LAYR constructs a conforming 3D mesh of triangular prisms—by first triangulating the plan view of bore locations and then extruding those surface triangles downward—to achieve smooth spatial interpolation of layered soil parameters both vertically and radially throughout the half‐space.

It is possible to define layered half-space with soil parameters and layer thickness varying in vertical as well as in the radial direction. Therefore each point at the soil-structure inter- face can have different soil-parameters associated to it. This is achieved by interpolating the
 soil-properties and layer thicknesses from the defined bore profiles. There are following inter- polation schemes available:
 1. CONS - Constant soil profile at all the points of the half-space
 2. QUAD - Bilinear interpolation of a separate system containing a discretized model of the soil
 3. COOR - Interpolation of bore profiles using weight functions
 4. LAYR - Interpolation of the soil properties from the 3D triangular prism mesh model of the layered half-space defined by the bore profile distribution on the half-space surface
 In the 2nd case (QUAD) an arbitrary mesh of QUAD elements (system 2) has to be defined. The contours of the soil profile are described by information stored at the nodes of this second mesh. The soil characteristics are then interpolated bilinearly from the QUAD elements of system 2 to the nodes of the structure in the primary system (structure node A is situated in QUAD element X of system 2; the soil characteristics of A are determined from the four corner profiles of the element X). In this way, irregular soil profile distributions can be defined easily. Also, the soil profile definition is independent of the numbering and organization of the structure contained in the primary system.
 In the 3rd case (COOR), vertical soil profiles are defined at coordinates (X1,Y1) to (Xnp,Ynp). Next, the soil characteristics of the nodes are calculated as the superposition of all bore profile properties c multiplied by a weight factor EP specified in the record HALF. As a rule, the closer a profile, the stronger its influence on a node (REP ) is:
 With this method, a variable soil profile distribution can be implemented quickly without the need for a secondary mesh. The bore profile input records can be easily inferred from the building site soil report.

 Fourth method (LAYR) first constructs the triangular mesh on the surface of the half-space from the defined bore-profiles (Figure 2.1a). Next this mesh is extruded along the axes of bore profiles to construct the three-dimensional mesh of triangular prisms, defining discreet soil (half-space) domain (Figure 2.1b). In this way soil-properties at the corner nodes of the triangular prism are exactly those defined by the corresponding BORE+BLAY record in AQUA. Stiffness and resistance properties within a prism are interpolated using hierarchical shape functions (linear in the radial, quadratic in the vertical direction). Variation of the soil-properties along the BORE axis defined in the BLAY record is preserved. Geometry of the 3D prism mesh is saved in an additional *CDB. The prisms are only used for the interpolation of the defined soil properties; they are not used for the computation of the stiffness matrix of the soil. Stresses and deformations and therefore the stiffness matrix are determined using the half- space theory (see Sections 2.4 and 2.5). All nodes that belong to the structure-soil interface (foundation plate, piles) must be entirely encompassed within defined half-space domain.
 Restrictions:
 • Minimum 3 bore profiles, whose start points describe a convex polygon.
 • For inclined bore profiles: intersection of the sides of prisms should be avoided.
 When specifying different soil characteristics in the plan view, the number of layers must be the same in all bore profiles. The layer thicknesses can vary, however. The values ES, MUE, PMAX, PMAL, C and PHI as well as the layer thicknesses are then interpolated according to either method 2, 3 or 4.
 If there is a large difference between the stiffness of two adjacent soil layers, numerical prob- lems may result. Then half-space theory is no longer applicable, and an error message is printed.

The sketch is a three-dimensional, schematic representation of a homogeneous half-space (soil or elastic medium) carrying a uniform circular surface load.  It is drawn as a large, upright cylinder whose curved side walls are hatched at the mid-height (left and right) to suggest that the material extends outward indefinitely (i.e. a “half-space”).  On the flat, top face of this cylinder:  

 • A uniformly applied pressure σ₀ (sigma-naught) is indicated by a callout arrow to the top surface.  
 • A dashed, concentric circle marks the boundary of the loaded area; its radius is denoted by r.  
 • At the very center of this dashed circle is an open circle symbol, identifying the “center point” beneath which stresses are being evaluated.  

Two orthogonal coordinate axes originate near the rim of the top surface:  
 • The X-axis projects horizontally to the right.  
 • The Y-axis is drawn diagonally downward and away from the viewing plane (giving a sense of 3D).  

From the open circle at the center of the loaded area, a dashed vertical line drops straight down through the interior of the cylinder.  At an arbitrary depth z below the surface, a small square block (or gauge symbol) is attached to that vertical line to denote the point at which the vertical stress σ_z (sigma-z) is being evaluated.  A bold arrow labeled σ_z points downward at that gauge, indicating the compressive vertical stress in the material at depth z.  The vertical line continues beneath the gauge, ending in a plain arrow pointing further downward (to indicate the positive z-direction is downward into the half-space).  

On the circumference of the curved side face of the cylinder, a series of short vertical arrows—each of equal length—point downward.  These represent the portion of the uniform circular surface load that “spills over” onto adjacent areas when the half-space is thought of as subdivided into nodes and load-areas.  In practice, each node would carry a circular patch of load whose radius r is determined (as described in the accompanying text) from the local finite-element mesh or manually for special foundations.

Overall, the drawing visually ties together the following theoretical elements:  
 1. The uniform surface pressure σ₀ applied over a circular area of radius r on an elastic half-space.  
 2. The coordinate system (X-Y in the surface plane, Z positive downward).  
 3. The vertical stress σ_z at any subsurface point (here, directly beneath the center) as a function of depth z.  
 4. The interpretation of loads at nodes and the distribution of those loads onto the half-space surface (illustrated by the array of downward arrows on the side wall).  

This illustration supports the classic Boussinesq/Smoltczyk formulation for stresses induced in a semi-infinite medium by a uniform circular pressure, as well as the transition to point‐load behavior outside the loaded radius and the interpolation in the transition zone.

The illustration consists of two schematic cross-sectional views of a homogeneous, isotropic half-space (e.g. soil) under vertical loading. Both sketches show the global Cartesian axes (x – horizontal, y – into the page, z – positive downwards), a small cubic “test volume” at an arbitrary subsurface point (x, y, z), and the notation used in Smoltczyk’s and Boussinesq’s vertical-stress formulas.

1. Diagram (a): Uniform Circular Surface Load  
   • A uniformly distributed pressure P acts downward over a circular area on the half-space surface.  
   • The center of the loaded area is taken as the origin (x =0, y =0, z =0). A bold vertical arrow labeled “P” marks the resultant concentrated load at the center.  
   • The boundary of the circular pressure patch is indicated by a dashed arc; the radius of that circle is marked “r.”  
   • From the center of load to the centroid of the test cube at depth is a solid slanted line labeled “R” (the straight‐line distance between load center and point (x,y,z)).  
   • The little cube encloses the point of interest, annotated “(x,y,z).” An upward arrow at the bottom face of the cube is labeled “σz,” denoting the vertical normal stress induced in the half-space at that point.  
   • The coordinate frame is shown with an x-axis arrow to the right, a y-axis arrow into the page (down‐left), and a z-axis arrow pointing downward.

2. Diagram (b): Concentrated Point Load on Surface  
   • The same half-space surface is now loaded by an idealized point load P acting at the origin. The load arrow “P” is again vertical and downward.  
   • A vertical dashed line along the z-axis from the surface down to the test cube is marked “z̄” (the depth coordinate of the point of interest).  
   • Two dashed/slanted lines connect the load application point to the cube:  
     – A solid-style slanted line labeled “R” (the direct distance from point load to (x,y,z̄)).  
     – A dashed-style slanted line labeled “R̄” (often interpreted as the horizontal radial distance or a related auxiliary length in the formula).  
   • The test cube again is annotated “(x,y,z̄),” and an upward arrow at its bottom face denotes “σz,” the computed vertical stress at that location under a point load.  
   • As before, axes x (horizontal), y (into page), and z (downwards) are shown.

Contextual Notes:  
– In classical half-space theory the circular load case (a) employs Smoltczyk’s closed-form expression for σz directly beneath the center of a uniformly loaded disk.  
– Outside the loaded radius r, the same pressure patch can be treated as a point load, so diagram (b) and the Boussinesq‐type formula for σz apply.  
– Variables used in the point‐load formula include Poisson’s ratio ν (often 0.35), normalized depths ζ = z/R, ζ̄ = z̄/R, and ρ = R̄/R.  
– In the transition zone (points within the disk but away from its center), stress values are interpolated between the two analytical solutions.  
– These stress distributions feed directly into strain calculations and settlement predictions, and can be stored or plotted at any desired depth via software routines (e.g. record SELP).

The illustration is a two-part schematic cross-section through a homogeneous, semi-infinite elastic half-space, showing how a single concentrated vertical load Pₖ applied at the ground surface produces both vertical strains εₓ (z) and vertical displacements s_z (z) at a subsurface observation point i directly beneath the surface.  

Overall geometry and axes  
• The ground surface is depicted by a heavy horizontal line at the top. A downward arrow at a point labeled k marks the applied concentrated load Pₖ on the surface.  
• A Cartesian coordinate system is shown with the horizontal x-axis running along the ground surface (an arrow to the right) and the vertical z-axis directed downward into the soil (an arrow at the left of the figure).  

Left panel: vertical strain distribution ε_z,i(z)  
• Directly beneath the load, at a horizontal distance from k, a vertical line labeled “i” indicates the ‘footprint’ of the observation point on the surface and its continuation downward.  
• The soil between that vertical line (through i) and a smoothly curved boundary to the right is filled with closely spaced, vertical hatching lines. This hatched region represents the volume of soil over which the load at k induces vertical strain at point i.  
• Within the hatched zone an oval annotation reads “ε_z,i(z)”, indicating the vertical strain at depth z along the line through point i.  
• The curved boundary, which bows outward away from the vertical line as depth increases, qualitatively reflects how the lateral extent of significant strain widens with depth under a point load.  

Right panel: vertical displacement distribution s_z,i(z)  
• A smaller, separate hatched region with the same curved-line geometry illustrates the corresponding vertical displacement (settlement) profile under the same load at point i.  
• An oval inside this region is labeled “s_z,i(z)”, identifying the settlement at depth z.  
• A small dot on the boundary of the hatched region marks a particular depth ẑ, and a callout next to it reads “s_z,i(ẑ)”, drawing attention to the displacement at that specific depth.  

Visual emphasis and conceptual link  
• Both panels use identical hatching and boundary shapes to reinforce that the strain ε_z,i(z) and displacement s_z,i(z) are computed along the same vertical trace through the soil at point i, but represent different physical quantities.  
• The smooth curved outline in each panel implies the classical elastic distribution predicted by the Boussinesq solution, in which both strains and displacements diminish with depth and spread laterally outward.  

Relation to context  
• This figure supports the discussion of the Boussinesq [3] method in the accompanying text: by integrating the vertical strain ε_z,i(z) from z = 0 down to some maximum depth, one obtains the total settlement s_z,i at the surface point i.  
• It visually underlines that, in the Boussinesq formulation, both vertical stresses σ_z and the sum of principal stresses (and thus horizontal stresses via Poisson’s ratio ν) contribute to the subsoil deformation field.

Also using a material input MNO in BLAY MNO, the value E in MAT...E is interpreted as stiffness property Es, nevertheless if MAT...MUE is defined or not.

Since the Poisson’s ration of the soil is hard to define and not a constant value, in most of the practical applications the Poisson’s ratio is directly taken into consideration by using the stiffness modulus Es instead of the elasticity modulus E (Smoltczyk [2]). For ν = 0 both moduli are formally identical:
 (1 − ν)
 $$Es = E * (1 + n)(1 - 2n) . (2.8)$$
 The vertical strains εz can now be obtained by simply dividing vertical stresses σz with stiffness modulus Es, i.e.
 σz(z)
 $$ez(z) = Es(z) . (2.9)$$
 This method is activated when Poisson’s ratio MUE in BLAY record is not defined or is equal to zero.

In addition to the vertical stiffness normally used in the description of the half-space, a hori- zontal stiffness can also be calculated and stored. This stiffness can be used to describe the horizontal fixities of the structure and must be given if no other horizontal fixities are defined.
 The horizontal stiffness is determined simply as a proportion of the vertical stiffness. If not specified in the record HALF no horizontal stiffness is stored.
 Vertical walls are not taken into account in the horizontal stiffness as they are shadowed for the more important z action - see next chapter. So horizontally only the lower bottom slabs work on friction as well as enbedded beams (external piles).
 A calculation of three-dimensional systems is possible only in the expanded version of HASE.

The figure is a schematic 2-D cross‐section through a pair of simply modeled “bottom slabs” and an upper slab (all shown in pale turquoise) used to illustrate how the HALF-ZVAR (variable Z-level halfspace) option handles contact nodes when slabs lie at different embedment depths. Key elements and their meaning are as follows:

1. Horizontal slabs and surface lines  
   • Two horizontal plate elements (light cyan) lie at different depths (“bottom slabs”). The left one is shallower; the right one lies about 4 m deeper.  
   • A continuous upper slab also spans from left to right at a higher Z-level.  
   • A red horizontal line drawn just above the left slab marks the user-defined global HALF-Z level: all elements above this height are forced “out of contact” with the halfspace.  
   • A green horizontal line above the right slab marks a locally assumed halfspace surface there, since no other higher slab is found in that neighborhood.

2. Contact‐node symbols  
   • Red circles along slab edges denote nodes where the code still applies an “active” halfspace stiffness (i.e. nodes lie in contact with the modeled soil halfspace).  
   • Green circles identify nodes that have been switched off—no halfspace contact—because they lie either above the global HALF-Z or fall into a “shadow” region cast by a higher slab.

3. Soil “shadow” wedge and 60° angle  
   • At the leftmost intersection of the bottom slab and a supporting wall, a dark blue 60° angle is drawn between the downward normal to the slab and an oblique line projected up and out. This illustrates the “shadowing” rule: soil beyond 60° from a slab edge is assumed inactive, and any nodes lying within that wedge are not given halfspace stiffness.  
   • The green-hatched triangular wedge immediately above the lower slab and behind the vertical wall represents the zone of soil that simply “rides” with the structure without contributing additional stiffness—nodes there turn green (no contact).

4. Wall and inactive soil zone  
   • A vertical structural wall element (outlined in thin black) connects the two slab levels. The soil in the triangular wedge between this wall and the lower slab, shaded with green diagonal stripes, is treated as inactive: it follows the slab and wall displacements rather than resisting them.  
   • This clearly isolates the active halfspace region (red-hatched below the lower slab) from the overlying soil that would otherwise be engaged.

5. Interpretation in a ZVAR context  
   • Because the two bottom slabs sit at different depths yet influence one another’s settlements, HASE’s ZVAR approach “scales” stiffnesses instead of using a single flat bedding layer.  
   • In the vicinity of the deeper (right) slab, no higher slab exists to cast a shadow, so a local (green) halfspace surface is assumed and contact nodes there remain active (red circles) except where they exceed HALF-Z.  
   • In contrast, above the left bottom slab and within its 60° shadow cone, nodes on the upper slab are turned off (green circles), accurately capturing the idea that that “overhead” soil does not press against the halfspace but deforms with the slab.

Overall, the diagram neatly visualizes: how global HALF-Z settings or local slab elevations define which nodes stay in contact; how the 60° shadow rule “turns off” contacts inside certain wedges; and how HASE-ZVAR automatically builds interaction between slabs at different Z-levels without resorting to a simple uniform bedding stiffness.

The figure presents a simplified longitudinal cross-section through a multi-support structure resting on variable-level soils, illustrating the principle of independent halfspace surfaces (HALF-ZVAR AUTO).  The overall color scheme helps distinguish structural elements, soil surfaces, and assumed halfspace contacts:

1. Structural elements and mesh  
   • On the far left, a reinforced concrete slab and basement wall are represented by a fine two-dimensional finite-element mesh (light cyan/blue lines).  The wall rises vertically from the slab and continues above grade.  
   • A continuous bridge deck or floor plate spans from left to right across the top of the image, drawn as a long line of regular quadrilateral mesh panels in medium blue.  
   • At mid-span, a single central support pier (column) is shown in darker grayish-green quadrilateral mesh.  Below this pier extends a cluster of three deep piles (thin vertical blue lines) driven into the halfspace.

2. Ground and environmental surfaces  
   • A gently undulating brown line represents the natural terrain surface (“environmental surface”) across the span, dipping down between the left slab and the central pier and then rising slightly to the right support.  
   • Beneath all structural elements is a pale blue fill indicating the underlying soil or halfspace volume.

3. Halfspace cutoff levels and local surfaces  
   • A horizontal solid red line is drawn at the elevation corresponding to the left bottom slab (the user-defined HALF-Z value).  This red line marks the global cutoff above which no halfspace contact is applied to elements; elements above this elevation are treated as if they lie outside the halfspace.  
   • Directly beneath this red line, a red inverted triangular symbol (pointing downward) highlights the location of the global halfspace contact plane.  
   • To the right, surrounding the central pier, a separate horizontal green line denotes a locally assumed halfspace surface.  A matching green triangle symbol identifies this local surface level.  Because no higher bottom slab exists nearby to shade it, the program assumes a distinct halfspace top at this elevation for the pier foundation and piles.  
   • Further to the right, at the right abutment, the same logic produces another short green segment under the footing, indicating yet another local halfspace cutoff.

4. Shadowing and interaction visualization  
   • From the lower-level slab on the left, a dashed 60° “shadow” boundary (not explicitly drawn but implied in the text) blocks any halfspace contact for nodes within the 60-degree cone above the slab.  The soil within this cone (below the green shaded region of the slab-and-wall intersection) is rendered inactive; it simply follows the deformation of the slab and wall above with no independent halfspace stiffness.  
   • The green shaded soil wedge between the cellar wall and the upper slab highlights this inactive volume.  If the user plots bedding stresses as iso-areas, this wedge appears as a zone of zero halfspace reaction, clearly demonstrating the shadowing effect of the lower slab on higher nodes.

5. Caption and figure notes  
   • Below the diagram, a caption reads “Figure 2.6: Independant halfspace surfaces,” emphasizing the concept that each bottom slab or foundation element may carry its own halfspace contact level when surrounded by other slabs at varying elevations.  
   • The interplay of red (global) and green (local) halfspace surfaces, combined with the shadowing rule, allows the HASE method to scale stiffnesses appropriately and capture interaction effects between slabs at different z-levels—effects that classical single-surface theories cannot represent.

Overall, this schematic clarifies how the HALF-ZVAR AUTO option detects neighboring higher slabs, switches off contact in their 60° shadow cones, and assigns either a global or local halfspace surface to each element. The visual cues—colored lines, mesh patterns, and triangular markers—make it straightforward to see where and why the halfspace contacts are activated or deactivated across the project’s varying elevations.

With the default HALF ZVAR AUTO also systems with quad halfspace contact on variable z level can be analyzed, see example hase3_variable_surface_level.dat
 Actually the halfspace theory is no longer valid exactly in such a case, but nevertheless the analysis with HASE also gives big advantages compared to a simple quad bedding. Because
 also in case of variable z level, e.g. a load on a bottom slab at z level 4m causes a settlement in a neighboring bottom slab at z level 8m, and the other way round, = interaction in the HASE stiffness coefficient method. HASE tries to scale the stiffnesses to get good results also if the quad halfspace contact acts on variable z levels.
 In principle, in case a quad bottom slab lies under the halfspace surface, all under 60 degree higher nodes above will not get a halfspace contact. According the following figure, from the lower bottom slab a shadow is assumed under an angle of 60 degree to switch off nodes above:
 The soil in the angle of the cellar wall and the upper slab (green shaded) is inactive and just follows the deformation of the upper slab and the wall. To check this effect of the ZVAR method please plot the bedding stress as iso-area and you will immediately see this shadowing.
 If no shadowing occurs, all bottom slabs work as if they would stand on the top of the halfspace. This es e.g. the case if the right abutment of a bridge has another l level as the left one but both lie on the surrounding terrain surface. So the program looks around a bottom slab if there are other higher bottom slabs around:
 - if yes, the deep bottom slab is assumed to lie inside the halfspace
 - if no, the bottom slab is assumed to lie on top of the surface (uses a separate surface level)
 So with HALF-Z you mainly define, which elements will definitely not get a halfspace contact (all elements above HALF-Z).

The same happens at the middle support with enbedded piles. So this represents the brown environmental surface.

There are two ways to model model load introduction by means of piles in HASE – as internal HASE-piles (PILE) or as extended piles (XPIL).
 Internal HASE-piles are not discretized in the finite element system. They are a property of the halfspace and defined with command PILE. Example - hase8_intern_piles.dat
 Extended piles are real beam elements in the system and thus need not to be defined with command PILE. Example - hase22_abutment_extended_piles.dat

Internal HASE Piles are no ream beam elememts and may be included as part of the calcula- tion of the stiffness matrix at the halfspace surface. In the linear calculation, it is assumed that MANT times the total pile load is transferred by pile skin friction (literal MANT in record PILE) and the rest as point pressure at the foot of the pile.
 The part of load supported by skin friction is evenly distributed, relative to the soil stiffnesses along the pile, over the length of the pile and integrated numerically.
 Loads introduced within the half-space are calculated according to equation 2.5.
 Piles within the half-space can only be calculated in the expanded version of HASE.

Piles are defined as beam-elements in the system that lie below the halfspace surface. In HASE, the stiffnesses of all beam nodes are obtained using the formula 2.5.
 In HASE, it is possible to directly include the effects of soil bedding on a pile- bedded structure, where piles are modeled as discrete beam elements and are part of the structure. The GRP record can be used to select beam groups where stiffness values should be calculated within the halfspace. In contrast to the PILE functionality, which condenses the total effect of the pile to a single stiffness at the point where the pile is attached to the structure, each node along an extended pile represents explicit degrees of freedom within the halfspace. This allows bedding effects to be represented continuously along the pile.
 The effective soil stiffness properties along X-pile are always determined from the half-space stiffness defined using bore profiles.
 If additional nonlinear resistance effects along X-pile are to be considered, this can be done by one of the following:
 1. Definition of the nonlinear resistance properties for each individual pile directly. If you do not need to give an individual nonlinear effect to every pile, the second method is recommended! If you need individual nonlinear effects this can be achieved by:
 • defining bedding profiles containing nonlinear specific information using BORE + BBAX or BBLA
 assigning these profiles directly to the corresponding X-pile beams at system input
 The following X-pile nonlinear effects can be taken into account when performing a non- linear analysis in combination with ASE:
 • maximum pile skin friction along the pile C0 (see AQUA record BBAX)
 • maximum axial pile foot force PMAX (see AQUA record BBAX)
 • maximum transverse compression PMA1 and PMA2 (see AQUA record BBLA)
 2. Interpolation of the nonlinear resistance properties from the corresponding soil parame- ters of the defined bore profile distribution. The length of the piles within halfspace, the pile diameter and pile circumference are automatically taken into consideration for the evaluation of the pile specific values. This method is achieved by:

• maximum transverse compression PMA1 and PMA2 (see AQUA record BBLA). 2. Interpolation of the nonlinear resistance properties from the corresponding soil parame- ters of the defined bore profile distribution. The length of the piles within halfspace, the pile diameter and pile circumference are automatically taken into consideration for the evaluation of the pile specific values. This method is achieved by:.
 •
 defining the soil nonlinear resistance properties using AQUA records BORE and BLAY
 •
 interpolating these properties using one of four interpolation schemes described in Section 2.3
 The X-pile nonlinear resistance properties that are interpolated in this way are maximum pressure at pile foot (PMAX), maximum lateral pressure (PMAL), cohesion (C) and soil- pile friction angle.
 Method 2 is a preferred method for the definition of X-pile resistance properties. Example: hase21_kpp_extended_piles.dat

Below is a concise, self-contained description of the chart in the image. It is written so that an AI-driven retrieval system (RAG) can index its key visual elements, data series, axis scales and annotations.

1. General overview  
   - The figure is titled “Figure 2.7: Memory requirement.”  
   - It presents four separate data series (labeled I, II, III and IV) showing how the main-memory requirement (in megabytes) grows with the number of half-space nodes in a boundary-element analysis.  
   - Each series corresponds to a different “influence radius” setting.

2. Axes  
   - Horizontal axis (x-axis): Number of half-space nodes.  
     • Tick marks and labels at approximately 500, 1 000, 2 000 and 3 000 nodes.  
   - Vertical axis (y-axis): Main-memory requirement in megabytes (MB).  
     • The vertical scale shows tick marks at 4 MB, 8 MB, 12 MB and 16 MB.  
     • The origin (0, 0) is located at the lower-left corner where both axes meet.

3. Data series and markers  
   - All four curves start close together near the origin (at low node counts), then diverge upward as node count increases.  
   - Each curve is drawn with straight line segments connecting data points. Each data point is marked with a circle enclosing an “×” (circled-cross marker).  
   - The four curves are annotated at their upper-right ends with Roman numerals I through IV. They ascend in order of steepness:
     • Curve I (steepest): Rises most sharply; at 2 000 nodes it already exceeds 14 MB, at 3 000 nodes it approaches or surpasses 16 MB.  
     • Curve II: Less steep than I but significantly steeper than III and IV; at 2 000 nodes it is around 12 MB, at 3 000 nodes approximately 13–14 MB.  
     • Curve III: Moderately steep; at 2 000 nodes it is near 8 MB, and at 3 000 nodes around 10–11 MB.  
     • Curve IV (flattest): Grows slowly; at 2 000 nodes roughly 5–6 MB, at 3 000 nodes about 7 MB.

4. Relation to influence radius  
   - According to the accompanying text, the curves represent different influence radii used in the computation:  
     • Curve I: Influence radius = 999 m (effectively full-domain coupling).  
     • Curve II: Radius = 30 % of system dimension.  
     • Curve III: Radius = 10 % of system dimension.  
     • Curve IV: Radius = 3 % of system dimension.

5. Interpretation  
   - As the influence radius shrinks (from I to IV), the bandwidth of the stiffness (flexibility) matrix is reduced, which directly lowers both the CPU time for inversion and the in-core memory requirements.  
   - The extreme case (Curve IV) remains under 8 MB even at 3 000 nodes, whereas full-domain coupling (Curve I) quickly demands 16 MB or more at the same node count.

This description captures the chart’s structure, each data series’ visual styling and numerical behavior, and its connection to the defined influence-radius parameters.

The following limits should be observed:
 Number of bore profiles : 999 Number of system nodes : 999999 Number of halfspace nodes : 65000 Greatest node number : 999999
 Further limits are imposed by HASE and also by the computer hardware.
 The stiffness matrix must be determined by inverting the flexibility matrix. In this case, the system of equations must be solved n times (where n = number of nodes in halfspace). By comparison, in ASE the system of equations must be solved for a load case only 1 time, but for m unknowns (for the plate this is m = 3n, as each node has 3 unknowns).
 Because the inversion step costs a lot of CPU time, it is executed only in-core, that means exclusively in the main memory. Therefore the number of nodes which can be calculated depends on the size of main memory available. It also depends on the band width of the system of equations. This can be reduced by lowering the influence radius with the record CTRL INFL. Reducing bandwidth naturally reduces CPU time. The memory requirements can be estimated with the following diagram. The curves I to IV show different influence radii:
 Curve I : Influence radius = 999m
 Curve II : Influence radius = 30% of the system dimension Curve III : Influence radius = 10% of the system dimension Curve IV : Influence radius = 3% of the system dimension
 A square plate with 16m16m and 4040 elements (4141 = 1681 nodes) needs approxi- mately 6 − 7MB main memory for an influence radius of 4.80m(= 30% of 16m). With 4MB main memory, the problem can be processed with a maximum influence radius of approxi- mately 3.00m.

The stiffness of the halfspace is saved by HASE in the file PROJECT.$E2.
 At the start of the following statics program (ASE), this $E2-file is read in using the command STEX. The stiffness of the superstructure is then combined with the stiffness matrix of the halfspace to form a total stiffness matrix. The system of equations is solved and saved as PROJEKT.$D1.
 The default argument of the STEX command is PROJECT.$E2, so the input of STEX without any argument is generally sufficient. Because the contact nodes of the halfspace are assigned external node numbers, any other $E2-file may alternatively be specified.
 In the following statics calculation, load cases can quickly be computed without having to re- solve the system of equations. The STEX command need only be specified once for multiple load cases. No group selection is allowed. If material values or similar values used as inputs to HASE are modified, the system of equations must be set up and solved again in HASE.

Input is written in text using the free format of the CADINP input language (see the general manual ’SOFiSTiK Basics’).
 Three categories of units are distinguished:
 mm Fixed unit. Input is always required in the specified unit.
 [mm] Explicit unit. Input defaults to the specified unit. Alternatively, an explicit as- signment of a related unit is possible (eg. 2.5[m] ).
 [mm]1011 Implicit unit. Implicit units are categorised semantically and denoted by a cor- responding identity number (shown in green). Valid categories referring to the unit ”length” are, for example, geodetic elevation, section length and thickness. The default unit for each category is defined by the currently active (design code specific) unit set. This input default can be overridden as described above. The specified unit in square brackets corresponds to the default for unit set 5 (Eu- rocodes, NORM UNIT 5).

The table shown defines a series of input “records” for SOFiSTiK’s HASE module.  Each record begins with a keyword (the left‐hand column) and is followed by a fixed list of data items (the right‐hand column).  The overall file is organized in “blocks” representing systems or load cases, each block ending with an END record.  An empty block (END/END) signals the end of the program run.  The general control records HEAD, END and PAGE are covered in the SOFiSTiK “Basics” manual and are not repeated here.

1. CTRL  
   • Keywords: OPT, VAL  
   • Usage: Global control options.  OPT selects a particular switch or feature, VAL supplies its numeric or character value.  Multiple CTRL records can redefine solver settings at different stages.

2. GRP  
   • Keywords: NO, VAL, FOOT, RC, CC  
   • Usage: Defines a grouping (NO = group number) with an associated value (VAL).  FOOT can carry a footing identifier; RC/CC might designate reinforcement class or cross‐section code.

3. HALF  
   • Keywords: TYPE, PROF, EP, Z, FAKX, FAKY, FAKZ, NAME  
   • Usage: Establishes a “half‐space” or layer.  TYPE selects the boundary condition type, PROF names a predefined profile, EP is thickness or modulus, Z gives elevation.  FAKX, FAKY, FAKZ are reduction or amplification factors in each axis.  NAME labels the half‐space for later reference.

4. BORE  
   • Keywords: NO  
   • Usage: Marks the start of a bore log definition, numbered by NO.  Further details for each borehole are specified in subsequent PILE records.

5. PILE  
   • Keywords: X, Y, D0, D, Z, MANT, ZMAN, PMAM, PMAF, MNO, TITL  
   • Usage: Describes pile or borehole geometry/material at a given location—  
      – X, Y: plan coordinates  
      – D0: initial diameter/top diameter  
      – D: design or bottom diameter  
      – Z: elevation of section  
      – MANT: material identifier for the annulus (mortar or soil)  
      – ZMAN: manual override for layering  
      – PMAM, PMAF: axial bearing resistance (maximum/minimum)  
      – MNO: reference to material number  
      – TITL: text title or comment

6. PLAS  
   • Keywords: PMAX  
   • Usage: Defines an ultimate plastic capacity or maximum allowable load (PMAX).

7. LOAR  
   • Keywords: NO, R  
   • Usage: Load area definitions—NO assigns the area ID, R sets a radial dimension or reference value.

8. LC  
   • Keywords: NO, NAME, TITL, STVZ  
   • Usage: Defines a new load case—  
      – NO: load‐case number  
      – NAME: short alphanumeric label  
      – TITL: descriptive title  
      – STVZ: switching flag for static vs. vibration analysis

9. LOAD  
   • Keywords: NO, PZ  
   • Usage: Assigns nodal or area loads under a specific load‐case number (NO).  PZ is the magnitude or directional component in the Z‐axis.

10. SELE  
   • Keywords: NO, Z  
   • Usage: Selects a result set or evaluation plane—NO is the selector ID; Z gives the elevation at which results are extracted.

11. SELP  
   • Keywords: Z, LCST, BRIC, DX, DY, HMIN  
   • Usage: Defines a regular grid or slice for postprocessing—  
      – Z: elevation of slice  
      – LCST: starting load‐case number to include  
      – BRIC: inclusion flag for brick‐element results  
      – DX, DY: grid spacing in X and Y  
      – HMIN: minimum element thickness to consider

12. ECHO  
   • Keywords: OPT, VAL  
   • Usage: Controls on‐screen or print‐out echoing of input definitions.  OPT chooses what to echo, VAL sets verbosity or destination.

Key Notes:  
• Blocks of these records must be terminated by an END record before a new system or load‐case block begins.  
• Any previously defined material values (for example via a MATERIAL record in the HASE environment) may be overridden here.  
• The file ends when an END/END (an END record followed immediately by another END) is encountered.  
• HEAD, END and PAGE are global control records documented separately in the “Basics” manual.

Previously defined material values may be modified in HASE.
 The input is ordered in blocks which are terminated by an END record. A particular system or a load case can be analyzed within each block. The program ends if an empty block (END/END) is found.

The input table defines the syntax and meaning of a two-row “keyword/value” record used to control the HASE solver’s behavior.  It has four columns – Item, Description, Unit and Default – and two items (“OPT” and “VAL”).  Below is a structured, detailed breakdown suitable for semantic ingestion into a RAG vector store:

1. Table Overview  
   • Name (implicit): OPT/VAL control record  
   • Purpose: Specify one or more solver control options (OPT) and assign them concrete values (VAL)  
   • Rows:  
     – OPT – lists the control keywords and their brief definitions  
     – VAL – holds the corresponding values for each keyword  

2. Columns  
   – Item (string)  
     • Indicates the record type: “OPT” for option definitions; “VAL” for their values  
   – Description (string)  
     • For OPT: a concise explanation of each keyword’s function  
     • For VAL: simply “Value of the option,” i.e. the user-supplied literal or number  
   – Unit (string)  
     • “LIT” for literal keywords (OPT row)  
     • “–” for the VAL row (values may be numeric, literal or flags)  
   – Default (string or number)  
     • The solver’s built-in default for each option (if any)  
     • “–” when no default is assigned or when user must supply  

3. OPT Row – Control Keywords  
   Each keyword is a literal token in the OPT record and may be followed by one or more values in the corresponding VAL record.

   a. INFL  
      • Full name: INFLUENCE radius for band width reduction  
      • Purpose: Nodes separated by more than INFL meters are assumed non-interacting.  This sparsifies the global stiffness matrix, cutting CPU time on large models.  
      • Default: 999 m  

   b. TOLS  
      • Full name: Minimum stiffness cutoff  
      • Purpose: Any computed stiffness smaller than (TOLS × maximum stiffness) is zeroed out instead of stored.  Improves sparsity.  
      • Default: 1.0 × 10⁻⁶  

   c. GAUS  
      • Full name: Number of Gauss integration points per soil sub-layer  
      • Purpose: Controls numerical integration accuracy of soil‐layer strains.  The program may subdivide thick layers automatically; setting GAUS = 1…3 adjusts the number of quadrature points.  
      • Default: 1  • Maximum allowed: 3  

   d. SOLV  
      • Full name: Solver mode  
      • Allowed values (case‐insensitive):  
         – 0  : Disable stiffness inversion; only collect nonlinear parameters for ASE (cf. “PLAS” record).  
         – (none)  : Default HASE behavior – compute flexibility matrix, invert it to stiffness.  May be time-consuming.  
         – NONL  : Skip inversion of flexibility matrix; rely on ASE to iterate (requires “ASE STEX OPT ITER”).  Can be faster overall.  
      • Default: (none, i.e. full linear solve)  

   e. FAKU  
      • Full name: Ignore tension caused by pile forces  
      • Purpose: Applicable only to HASE‐type pile elements (PILE).  Automatically computes how much pile load is transmitted downward into a rigid subsoil rather than as upward tension.  That portion is reported in the “faku” column of the pile parameter output.  
      • Special usage:  
         – “CTRL FAKU 1” forces 100% of pile skin friction and tip loads to act downward (pure compression).  
      • Default: Automatic (soil-profile based)  

   f. WARN  
      • Full name: Switch off error messages  
      • Purpose: Suppresses non-fatal warnings during preprocessing and solution.  
      • Default: messages on (i.e. WARN is off)  

4. VAL Row  
   – Item: VAL  
   – Description: “Value of the option”  
   – Unit: –  
   – Default: –  
   – Content: The user-supplied literal or numerical value(s) corresponding to each keyword listed in OPT.  

Summary  
This compact two-row table allows users to define up to six solver control keywords (OPT) in one record and then immediately list their assigned values (VAL).  Each keyword comes with a clear purpose, unit context (meters, relative tolerance, quadrature count, literal mode flags) and default behavior.

A finer subdivision of these integration layers leads to improvements in accuracy of only few percent in most cases. Default: GAUS = 1, maximum value: GAUS=3
 SOLV CTRL SOLV 0 : to switch off the calculation to only store non-linear parameters for ASE (see record PLAS).

 FAKU Piles in the halfspace: Works only on PILE (HASE-piles) and not on extended piles (real beam elements):
 If a pile foot stands on a rigid subsoil, it transmits its load directly downward and not partially as tension upward (as the equation [1] for a load which acts in the halfspace interior would suggest). Based on the soil profile (the actual available stiffnesses), HASE automatically determines how much of the pile load is diverted directly downward. Then this part produces no tension upward. It is output as “faku” in the table of pile parameters. For special cases, a minimum value can be defined with FAKU - when CTRL FAKU 1 is set, that means all pile forces (also the skin friction forces) are transmitted downward as compression.

content:
The table presented defines five input items (parameters) that control group selection, result‐output behavior and the way “pile‐foot” stiffness and contact properties are modeled in a geotechnical analysis program (e.g. HASE).  Each parameter is described below in terms of its purpose, allowed values, units and default setting.  Where relevant, additional notes from the accompanying text are included.

1. NR (Group Number)  
   • Description: Identifies which group or groups of elements are to be activated.  
     – ALL: a special keyword meaning “all groups are selected.”  
   • Unit: – (unitless) or LIT (literal text).  
   • Default: “!”  (an exclamation mark denotes the program’s internal default group selection, typically all groups when no other input is given.)  
   • Notes: In the absence of any NR input, all elements / groups are assumed active.  When you do supply NR, only those group numbers listed are used.

2. VAL (Option Flag)  
   • Description: Controls whether element results are used and whether they are written to output.  
     – OFF: do not use this group (results are ignored).  
     – YES: use the group in calculations but do not write their results to the output file.  
     – FULL: use the group and write its results to the output file.  
   • Unit: LIT (literal text).  
   • Default: FULL  
   • Notes: This flag lets you tailor which groups contribute to the analysis and which of those contribute visible output, enabling streamlined result files.

3. FOOT (X-Pile Foot Radius)  
   • Description: Specifies the radius (or effective diameter) of the pile‐foot (pile toe) to simulate additional stiffness at the base of a pile element.  
   • Unit: meters (m).  
   • Default: –1.0  
   • Interpretation:  
     – If FOOT is positive, it is taken directly as the pile‐foot radius in meters.  
     – If FOOT is negative, its absolute value is a multiplier of the (equivalent) pile radius.  For example, FOOT = –1.4 means the pile‐foot radius is 1.4 × pile radius.  
   • Notes: The program by default uses a pile‐foot diameter 1.4 × the pile’s equivalent diameter (hence default of –1.0 often corresponds internally to –1.4 when no override is given, or vice versa according to version).  Use FOOT to adjust the stiffness contribution of the pile base.

4. RC (Contact Radius for Stiffness)  
   • Description: Overrides the automatically computed contact radius used in stiffness calculations between the pile and surrounding soil.  
   • Unit: meters (m).  
   • Default: – (no override).  
   • Notes: When RC is unspecified, HASE computes the contact radius from the pile geometry.  Supplying RC forces the use of your value instead.

5. CC (Contact Circumference for Nonlinear Mantle Friction)  
   • Description: Overrides the automatically computed contact circumference used in modeling nonlinear skin friction along the pile shaft (mantle).  
   • Unit: meters (m).  
   • Default: – (no override).  
   • Notes: As with RC, omitting CC leaves the program to derive the circumference from the pile’s cross‐section.  Providing CC applies your specified value.

––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––  
Additional Context  
• See also: CTRL, GRP commands/models in HASE.  
• Without any input parameters, all groups are used with default stiffness and contact properties.  As soon as specific NR, VAL, FOOT, RC or CC values are supplied, only those explicitly defined groups or overrides are applied, giving the user fine control over which elements participate, how their results are output, and how pile‐foot and contact interactions are represented.

See also: CTRL
 GRP
 All elements are used if nothing is input. When there is input, only the specified groups get activated.
 To simulate the effects of additional stiffness at the pile foot, the (positive) diameter of the pile foot can be specified with FOOT. Alternatively, the pile foot diameter can be specified as a multiple of the pile diameter (where the pile diameter is calculated as an equivalent diameter, from the pile cross-section area), in which case the FOOT value is flagged with a minus sign. The default pile footing is 1.4 times the pile diameter, or −1.4.
 With the input of the options RC and CC the user is able to overwrite the values of the contact radius and contact circumference which are computed by HASE automatically.

The table governs the definition of a subgrade “half-space” bedding—its geometry, layering, and contact stiffness—in a finite-element (QUAD) model. Each row (“Item”) names a parameter, its meaning (“Description”), its physical or logical units (“Unit”), and the default value used when the keyword is omitted.

1. TYPE (unit: LIT, default = CONS)  
  – Determines how the soil layering or half-space thickness is distributed in plan view. Three modes are supported:  
    • CONS  
      Constant profile everywhere. The half-space has uniform layer thicknesses and identical material parameters throughout.  
    • COOR  
      Interpolation of borehole profiles. Actual soil horizons are interpolated between bore coordinate points using a weight factor EP. A user-supplied profile file (e.g. hase5_profile_interpolation.dat) must be provided.  
    • LAYR  
      Layered half-space derived from a discrete 3D triangular-prism mesh. Stiffness and resistance parameters (from a BLAY soil library) are interpolated across layers defined by the bore profile. The mesh geometry is written to a secondary database (CDB) file whose name is given by NAME or defaults to “(project_name)_yr.cdb.”  

2. EP (unit: —, default = 1.5)  
  – Weight factor used only when TYPE = COOR. Controls how strongly borehole data influence the interpolated soil surface elevations and layer depths in plan. A higher EP concentrates the interpolation nearer the sample points.  

3. Z (unit: m, default = 0)  
  – Elevation of the half-space contact surface in the global coordinate system. All quads (2D elements) whose reference depth lies above Z lie in free air; below Z they interact with the half-space according to bedding definitions and stiffness factors.  

4. ZVAR (unit: LIT, default = AUTO)  
  – Switch for variable surface elevation behavior (see Chapter 2). Two options:  
    • NO  
      Elements (QUADs) wholly below Z are ignored—no contact enforced.  
    • AUTO  
      Even horizontal QUADs below Z maintain half-space contact, allowing a variable topography that adapts automatically.  

5. FAKX, FAKY, FAKZ (unit: —, defaults = 0.4, 0.4, 1.0)  
  – Directional stiffness factors (spring-type contacts) in the X, Y, and Z axes, respectively. These dimensionless multipliers scale the normal and shear stiffness of the soil half-space against the overlying elements:  
    • FAKX, FAKY affect horizontal resistance (chap. 2: Horizontal Stiffness)  
    • FAKZ governs vertical resistance  

6. NAME (unit: LIT32, default = “–”)  
  – Specifies the file name for a secondary QUAD database or the newly generated LAYR database. If TYPE = LAYR and no NAME is provided, the system writes the mesh to “(project_name)_yr.cdb.”  

See also related keywords in pre- and post-processing: CTRL, LOAR, LC, LOAD, PLAS. These control global settings, load definitions, and plasticity models that may interact with or override bedding parameters.

See also: CTRL, LOAR, LC, LOAD, PLAS
 HALF
 For TYPE CONS, the halfspace in the plan view has constant layer thicknesses, with each layer containing uniform material parameters.
 For TYPE COOR, a variable profile distribution can be defined based on interpolation of bore profiles (see Section 2.3). Example: hase5_profile_interpolation.dat
 For TYPE LAYR soil properties (stiffness and resistance values from BLAY) are interpolated from the discrete model of a layered half-space (3D triangular prism mesh) defined automati- cally by a bore profile definition (see Section 2.3). The geometry of this 3D mesh is saved in an additional database under a file name specified with item NAME. If no name is given, then the newly created *CDB will be saved under a name $(nme)_yr.cdb, where $(nme) stands for the name of the current project. Example: hase4_layr_interpolation.dat
 A horizontal bedding can be simulated with FAKX and FAKY. For FAKX and FAKY see chapter 2: Horizontal Stiffness.

The table shown is a concise definition of the single parameter used by the BORE record in the HASE module (which in turn draws on bore-profile definitions supplied via AQUA). It tells the system how many bore profiles the user explicitly selects for defining a half-space interpolation. Below is a breakdown of each column and row entry, together with its role in the broader context of the four interpolation schemes (CONS, QUAD, COOR, LAYR).  

1. Table-Level Context  
– Purpose:  Specify the number of bore profiles to include in the half‐space definition.  
– Scope:  Applies only when using the BORE record together with HASE’s half‐space routines.  
– Relation to interpolation types:  
  • CONS:  Only one profile can actually be used; the count (NO) may still be set but only the smallest‐numbered profile is active.  
  • QUAD:  BORE is ignored; all profiles tied into AQUA → QUAD are automatically used.  
  • COOR:  Requires at least two profiles (NO ≥ 2); if unspecified, all AQUA profiles are taken.  
  • LAYR:  Requires at least three profiles (NO ≥ 3); if unspecified, all AQUA profiles are taken.  

2. Column Descriptions  
– Item  
  • Label for the parameter. Here it is “NO.”  
  • This is the keyword users place on the BORE card to indicate they are specifying a count.  

– Description  
  • A textual explication: “Numbers of selected bore profiles.”  
  • It informs the user that this field directly controls how many profiles are being flagged for half-space interpolation.  

– Unit  
  • Shown as “—” because this is a dimensionless count (an integer).  
  • No physical units apply.  

– Default  
  • The entry “!” signals that NO is mandatory whenever a BORE record is provided.  
  • There is no implicit default numeric value; the user must supply one.  

3. Row: NO  
– Parameter name: NO  
– Meaning: The integer count of bore profiles the user explicitly selects.  
– Constraints by interpolation type:  
   • CONS: Although you can supply NO, only one profile will be applied. If NO ≠ 1, the system still defaults to the smallest profile index.  
   • QUAD: NO is ignored—don’t supply it if QUAD interpolation is in use.  
   • COOR: Enforce NO ≥ 2. If NO is omitted, the system reverts to using every bore profile known in AQUA.  
   • LAYR: Enforce NO ≥ 3, otherwise an error or fallback to “all profiles” occurs.  
– Use in practice: Set NO equal to the exact number of profiles you wish to draw from — for example, NO = 2 for a COOR run, NO = 3 or more for LAYR.  

4. Practical Notes  
– If you accidentally omit NO on a BORE record, HASE will either:  
   • For CONS: pick profile #1 automatically.  
   • For COOR or LAYR: use every defined AQUA profile, potentially leading to a heavier computation.  
– Supplying NO greater than the available profiles triggers a runtime error.  
– For QUAD‐based interpolation, simply omit the BORE record altogether.  

By documenting the “NO” field in this way, the table equips users and downstream RAG-vector workflows to parse, validate, and index the parameter consistently across different half‐space interpolation modes.

See also: HALF
 BORE
 The record BORE specifies which bore profiles defined in AQUA are to be used by HASE for the definition of the halfspace. Depending on the type of the interpolation, the following applies:
 1. CONS - For this type of interpolation only one bore profile will be used for the definition of the halfspace. If BORE record is not specified, then a bore profile with smallest bore profile number (as defined in AQUA) will be selected. Similarly if more than one bore profile is defined with BORE record, bore profile with smallest bore profile number will be used.
 2. QUAD - BORE record is not used for this interpolation type. All bore profiles which are defined with AQUA and used for the generation of the secondary QUAD system will also be used for the definition of the halfspace.
 3. COOR - Minimum two bore profiles must be specified with BORE record. If nothing is specified, all bore profiles defined within AQUA are used for the interpolation.
 4. LAYR - Minimum three bore profiles must be specified for this method to be applied. As before, if nothing is specified, all bore profiles defined within AQUA are used.

The table shown is the definition of the PILE input record in HASE-3D, describing how internal piles are represented in a half-space analysis. Internal piles in HASE are not modeled as discrete beam elements but as a modification of the half-space stiffness at surface nodes. Loads on these piles are resolved into skin-friction along their shaft and a concentrated pile-foot reaction at their base. In linear analyses the total pile load is split by the fraction MANT into skin-friction and by (1 – MANT) into pile-foot reaction; in nonlinear analyses these components are likewise transferred but are capped individually by PMAM and PMAF (see record PLAS for detailed nonlinear behavior). Below is a detailed description of each table entry:

1. Item X  
   • Description: Either the horizontal coordinate of the pile head (in metres) or, when prefaced by “NNO,” the surface node number at which the pile interacts with the half-space.  
   • Unit: m  
   • Default: mandatory input (!)

2. Item Y  
   • Description: Either the second horizontal coordinate of the pile head (in metres) or, when prefaced by “NNO,” again the same node number as X.  
   • Unit: m  
   • Default: mandatory input (!)

3. Item D0  
   • Description: The nominal pile diameter used to compute the concrete cross-section A = π·(D0/2)². This influences the axial stiffness EA and the distribution of skin-friction.  
   • Unit: m  
   • Default: mandatory input (!)

4. Item D  
   • Description: The diameter of the pile base. Under settlement, the effective vertical stress is computed directly beneath the pile foot using this diameter.  
   • Unit: m  
   • Default: automatically set to D0 (or to D0/1.5 if a special notation “!/1.5D0” is used)

5. Item Z  
   • Description: The depth coordinate of the pile foot (pile tip) below the ground surface.  
   • Unit: m  
   • Default: mandatory input (!)

6. Item MANT  
   • Description: The fraction of the total axial pile load that is carried by skin-friction along the shaft. The remaining fraction (1 – MANT) is carried at the pile foot.  
   • Unit: – (dimensionless)  
   • Default: 0.50

7. Item ZMAN  
   • Description: The start depth (below the surface) at which skin-friction is considered active. Above this depth the relative soil–pile displacements are assumed too small to mobilize friction. By default, the top 25% of the pile length is inactive.  
   • Unit: m  
   • Default: set internally to 25% of pile length (noted by “*”)

8. Item PMAM  
   • Description: The maximum axial load that can be transferred by skin-friction (kN). Only applies in nonlinear analyses.  
   • Unit: kN  
   • Default: none (–)

9. Item PMAF  
   • Description: The maximum axial load that can be passed through the pile foot (kN). Only applies in nonlinear analyses.  
   • Unit: kN  
   • Default: none (–)

10. Item MNO  
    • Description: Material number to be assigned to the concrete piles. If specified, the Young’s modulus of that material is used; otherwise a default E = 28 000 MN/m² (C30/37 concrete) is assumed.  
    • Unit: –  
    • Default: none (–)

11. Item TITL  
    • Description: A text identifier or designation for the pile (up to 16 characters).  
    • Unit: –  
    • Default: blank or user-defined

Additional Context Notes:  
- Internal HASE-piles (PILE record) alter only the stiffness matrix entries of the half-space surface nodes; they are not mesh elements.  
- Pile precompression settlement is accounted for by Δl = N·l/(E·A).  
- For extended pile modeling (beam-element piles), see the XPIL record and example “hase22_abutment_extended_piles.dat.”  
- The PILE record is available only in the expanded HASE-3D version.  
- For nonlinear soil behavior and limit definitions, consult record PLAS.

The figure is a simple 2-D cross-sectional sketch entitled “Figure 3.1: HASE Piles,” illustrating how internal HASE-piles are represented in the halfspace model. It is a black-and-white line drawing showing two idealized piles penetrating a uniform soil halfspace. Key features and labels include:

1. Ground surface  
   - A single horizontal line across the top of the drawing marks the soil/air interface (the halfspace surface).

2. Pile geometry  
   - On the left is a slender, unfilled (hollow) rectangular profile, representing a pile element of total length “L.”  
   - Immediately to its left, a vertical dimension line with arrowheads at both ends indicates L from the ground surface down to the pile tip.  
   - Partway down that same pile, a shorter vertical dimension line (bracketed on the left) marks the depth “ZMAN.” This shows the upper limit below which skin-friction is assumed to develop; above ZMAN, little or no frictional resistance is mobilized.

3. Skin-friction indicator (MANT)  
   - On the right is a second pile profile, drawn as a solid (filled) rectangle of the same length.  
   - Along its right face a bold upward-pointing arrow is shown, labeled “MANT.” This arrow denotes the distributed skin-friction component that the soil exerts on the pile shaft in the nonlinear analysis. The upward direction indicates that frictional shear resistance along the shaft opposes downward movement of the pile.  

4. Pile tip (foot) component  
   - Beneath the right-hand pile, the soil zone is lightly sketched to suggest the local stress distribution immediately below the pile tip. Although not explicitly labeled, this region corresponds to the “pile foot component” discussed in the text.  

5. Notation and context  
   - The overall pile length is L; ZMAN defines the depth from the ground surface below which skin friction is activated in the model.  
   - MANT is the notation used in HASE to specify the magnitude of the shaft‐friction parameter.  
   - No beam or frame elements are drawn – these piles are “internal” to the halfspace model. Their mechanical influence is applied via alterations to the soil stiffness matrix rather than explicit finite‐element discretization.  

Overall, the sketch summarizes how an internal HASE-PILE record imposes:  a) a zero-friction zone from surface to ZMAN; b) a distributed skin-friction load (MANT) along the pile shaft; and c) a concentrated end-bearing (foot) component at the pile tip, all embedded within an unbounded elastic halfspace.
