 There are two ways to model model load introduction by means of piles in HASE – as internal HASE-piles (PILE) or as extended piles (XPIL).
 Internal HASE-piles are not discretized in the finite element system. They are a property of the halfspace and defined with command PILE. Example - hase8_intern_piles.dat
 (to comare: extended piles see example - hase22_abutment_extended_piles.dat)
 With PILE defined internal piles are not real beam elements but have an impact on the stiffness coefficients calculated for nodes on the halfspace surface. In a linear calculation, it is assumed that the the total pile load is transferred to the soil, by means of a skin friction component (given by MANT) and a pile foot component. In a nonlinear calculation, loads are transferred similarly to the soil, but with the restriction that the limits specified by PMAM/PMAF may not be
 The skin friction is distributed over the length of the pile relative to the soil stiffnesses starting at depth ZMAN, and then numerically integrated. With the ZMAN record, it is possible to simulate that barely any force is transferred by the pile into the ground immediately beneath the bottom plate due to the small relative displacements at shallow depths. The loading occurs inside
 the halfspace according to: [1], p. 195 Halfspace Solution according to Midlin. This divides a load in the halfspace into a downward compressive stress component and an upward tensile stress component.
 The pile precompression is taken into account with Äl=N.l/EA when calculating settlements. The exact normal force distribution is used here with a fixed concrete elastic modulus of 28000 MN/m2 (C30/37). The concrete surface A is calculated from the diameter.
 If a material number is defined for the piles, the elastic modulus of that material is used for the analysis (e.g. for vibrated piles). If a material number is not given, an elastic modulus of 28000 MN/m2 is used for the analysis.

The table below summarizes the three non-linear halfspace parameters that can be specified in ASE’s PLAS and PILE records. These parameters control how the model treats soil compression, pile load limits and slab–soil interaction when you switch on non-linear behavior (e.g. in load cases 22, 23, etc.). If you only change PMAX, DPDS or the PILE limits, you can write them into the existing HASE database (project.$e2) with a “CTRL SOLV 0” command and then invoke ASE’s non-linear solver without recomputing the linear stiffness matrices. However, changing PILE MANT (the PMAM/PMAX ratio) does affect the linear stiffness, so it should be determined under the expected service load before any non-linear run.

Table: Non-linear input parameters for ASE  
| Item  | Description                                                                   | Unit    | Default |
|-------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------|---------|
| PMAX  | Maximum bedding stress at the boundary of the halfspace, i.e. the initial cap on compressive soil pressure under the bottom plate. This value is used directly if no DPDS is specified. | kN/m²  | –       |
| DPDS  | Exponential growth exponent for the bedding stress: the maximum allowable σₙ starts at PMAX right at the slab edge and then increases into the slab’s interior according to  
  σₙ(x) = PMAX·e^(DPDS·x)  
where x is distance from the edge (in meters). This allows you to simulate soil cohesion/friction effects without explicitly entering φ and C. | –       | –       |
| MUE   | Shear (friction) coefficient between the bottom slab and halfspace for horizontal loading. It governs horizontal sliding resistance in non-linear analyses. | –       | 0.5     |

Detailed parameter behaviors and interplay:

1. PMAX (record PLAS)  
 • Defines a uniform, positive compressive stress capacity under the entire slab if DPDS = 0.  
 • If DPDS is specified, PMAX applies only at the slab edge—further in, the cap on soil pressure grows exponentially.  
 • Example: PMAX = 40 kN/m², DPDS = 1.8  
  – At boundary (x = 0 m): σₙ = 40 kN/m²  
  – At x = 0.25 m: σₙ ≈ 40·e^(1.8·0.25) ≈ 63 kN/m²  
  – At x = 1.00 m: σₙ ≈ 40·e^(1.8·1.00) ≈ 240 kN/m²  

2. DPDS (record PLAS + DPDS)  
 • Simulates a φ–C soil model by gradually relaxing the bedding cap from the slab edge inward.  
 • Useful for capturing “plasticizing” near internal openings or slab gaps without subdividing the mesh.  

3. MUE (record PLAS)  
 • Controls the onset of slip between slab and soil under lateral loads.  
 • Default 0.5 can be adjusted up or down based on the expected friction angle and contact condition.  

Pile-related notes (records PILE and optionally PILE MANT):  
 • Compression limit at pile nodes = PMAM + PMAF (skin friction + toe resistance).  
 • Tensile limit at pile nodes = PMAM only.  
 • If either component is exceeded before the total pile capacity, ASE invokes plastic yielding at that node and deformations grow non-linearly. If the combined limit is reached, the pile “pushes” into the soil.  
 • Changing only PMAM/ PMAF/PMAX can be updated without re-computing linear stiffness (“CTRL SOLV 0”). Changing the PMAM/PMAX ratio via PILE MANT requires a fresh linear stiffness run.

See also: CTRL, HALF, PILE
 PLAS
 Non-linear halfspace calculations:
 The program ASE can be used to analyse the lifting of the bottom plate in a non- linear calcu- lation, as well as plasticizing at the plate edge and at the pile nodes.
 The record PLAS can be used to input a maximum soil pressure PMAX in kN/m2 for the bottom plate (which is valid over the entire halfspace). The input value represents a positive compressive stress.
 The following parameters can be specified for nonlinear calculations in ASE:
 • at halfspace nodes:
 compression: on input of PLAS: max. bedding max-sigma = PMAX (record PLAS)
 compression: with input of PLAS+DPDS you can simulate a phi and C of a soil. The max. bedding max-sigma can then increase starting from the boundary. Directly at the boundary, max-sigma starts with PLAS, to the interior of the slab max-sigma then increases with an e-function.
 Example PLAS=40 DPDS=1.8
 At the boundary: max-sigma =PLAS =40 kN/m2
 0.25 m inside: max-sigma 40 kN/m2*e0.25∗1.8 = 63 kN/m2
 1.00 m inside: max-sigma 40 kN/m2*e1.00∗1.8 = 240 kN/m2
 This DPDS e-function also works inside a slab e.g. at an internal gap as shown in example hase1_bottomslab.dat in loadcase 21 (linear) and 22 (nonlinear).
 tension: no tensile forces between the halfspace and the slab
 • at pile nodes:
 compression: max. pile force = PMAM+PMAF (record PILE)
 tension: max. pile force = PMAM (tensile piles)

The table shown is a small excerpt of an input‐deck parameter reference, defining two parameters (“Item”) that control how point‐loads are applied in a finite‐element model.  Below is a structured, human‐readable breakdown suitable for ingestion into a Retrieval‐Augmented Generation (RAG) vector store:

1. Table Structure  
   - Columns:  
     • Item: the keyword or identifier used in the input file.  
     • Description: a short text explaining the role of the parameter; sub‐entries indicate variants or levels.  
     • Unit: the physical units expected for the value (or a mnemonic for a special format).  
     • Default: the default value assigned if the user does not explicitly provide one.  

2. Cross‐References  
   - “See also: HALF, LOAR” implies related parameters or macros in the same input system, which can refine or override aspects of load application.  

3. Detailed Parameter Descriptions  

   A. Item = NO  
      – Purpose: Selects the node‐numbering scheme (and associated default minimum “load radius” behavior) for locating where concentrated loads will be applied.  
      – Unit: LIT  
         • LIT indicates that the argument to NO is to be read as a list identifier or literal token rather than a physical quantity.  
      – Default: 1  
         • If the NO keyword is omitted, node set “1” is assumed.  
      – Sub‐entries under “Description”:  
         • ALL  
             · Definition: When you choose NO = ALL, the same minimum load radius, R, is enforced on every node in the model.  
             · Default radius: 0.01 m  
               – Even if the user supplies R explicitly, the code will not let the radius fall below this floor for “ALL” nodes.  
         • BEAM  
             · Definition: Using NO = BEAM restricts the minimum radius enforcement only to nodes that belong to beam elements.  
             · Default radius: 0.25 m  
               – This larger default helps avoid numerical singularities when projecting loads onto 1D‐type (beam) elements.  

   B. Item = R  
      – Purpose: Specifies the “load radius,” i.e., the radius of the cylindrical (or spherical) influence zone around each selected node over which a point‐load is distributed.  
      – Unit: m  
         • This is a straightforward metric dimension.  
      – Default: !  
         • The exclamation mark denotes that no single global default is assumed here; instead, the radius falls back to the minimum values defined for ALL or BEAM when NO is used.  

4. Usage Notes  
   - The NO parameter must appear before specifying R if you rely on the ALL vs. BEAM minimums.  
   - If you explicitly set R to a larger value, that user‐supplied radius will override the 0.01 m or 0.25 m minimums, provided it remains physically reasonable.  
   - Cross‐references to HALF or LOAR may permit you to split the model into symmetrical halves or load arrays, respectively—check those sections for how they interact with NO and R.  

This description captures the purpose, defaults, units, and internal logic of the NO and R parameters, making it straightforward to index, retrieve, and explain in an automated help or RAG‐driven FAQ.

The table at hand defines the four fields of an LC (load-case) record in the HASE settlement-analysis pre-/post-processor.  Each field controls how results are stored and labeled in the HASE database, and interacts with the two available calculation modes (halfspace evaluation of an existing statics result vs. an independent settlement calculation).  Below is a field-by-field breakdown, followed by a brief synopsis of relevant context.  

1.  NO  (Load case number)  
   • Type/Unit: none (integer index)  
   • Default: 1  
   • Meaning: Unique identifier for this particular load case.  All results (stresses, displacements, bedding reactions, etc.) that HASE computes or imports under this LC record are tagged with NO.  In mode 2 (independent settlement calculation with explicit loads), if you reuse an existing NO, the old results under that case number are overwritten.  If you enter NO = 0, no results are saved.  

2.  NAME  (Database name of the results)  
   • Type/Unit: LIT32 (up to 32-character text)  
   • Default: “*” → current project name  
   • Meaning: Controls which database the result set is written into (or read from).  By default, HASE writes into the active project database.  However, if you want to pull in or append to results belonging to another database, you supply that database’s name here.  When reading from an external database, HASE expects that the “support forces” (i.e. the half-space reactions) have already been computed there; it matches data via external node numbering.  

3.  TITL  (Load case title)  
   • Type/Unit: LIT24 (up to 24-character text)  
   • Default: “*” → none (automatic)  
   • Meaning: A free‐form descriptive label for this load case.  If you are importing results from an external database, HASE will propose the designation already stored there—but you can override it with TITL.  In calculation mode 2 (independent settlement calculation), entering TITL is mandatory, because there is no statics program to supply a default label.  

4.  STVZ  (Load case number for saving half-space u-z displacements)  
   • Type/Unit: none (integer index)  
   • Default: 1  
   • Meaning: Only applies in non-linear analyses when you select calculation mode 1 (post-processing of a previously calculated halfspace).  By specifying STVZ, you tell HASE to write the vertical displacements of the half-space surface (u-z) into a separate load case.  This displacement may differ from the bottom-plate displacement that ASE reports, because in non-linear soil behavior the plate can lift off (tension) or sink further (plasticization).  STVZ must be distinct if you wish to compare those two displacement fields side by side (for example, as shown in the “Bottom Plate Non-linear Lift and Plasticizing” example Hase9.dat).  

Context of use:  
•  Two calculation modes exist for an LC record:  
   – Mode 1: Statics‐driven halfspace calculation (no LOAD records permitted).  HASE reads an existing halfspace solution from a prior HASE calculation (HASE file), imports the building’s support reactions from an external statics program (through the current or external NAME), evaluates bedding stresses in the halfspace, and stores them.  If any QUAD beddings are defined in parallel, bedding-stress storage is disabled to prevent data‐structure collisions.  
   – Mode 2: Independent settlement calculation (requires a HALF record plus explicit LOAD records).  HASE builds its own halfspace model, applies node‐wise loads you supply, performs the settlement analysis, and writes displacements and stresses tagged by NO and titled by TITL.  Previous results under the same NO are purged unless NO = 0.  

By correctly populating NO, NAME, TITL and (optionally) STVZ, you control where and how HASE records both linear and non-linear halfspace results for subsequent retrieval, graphical output, or comparison with other programs such as WING.

The table defines the syntax and parameters for the “LOAD” record used in standalone settlement analyses of a half-space model. Whenever a user issues a LOAD command under a particular load case number (LC), the software ignores any finite-element (FE) stiffness contributions and treats the specified loads purely as untensioned pressures acting on the half-space QUAD elements. If a load case with the same LC number already exists, it is automatically overwritten by the new LOAD record.

Below is a structured, detailed description of each table field and how it integrates into the settlement‐only workflow:

1. Item: NO  
   • Description: Specifies the node number from which the load is applied.  
     – In normal use, this refers to the identifier of a single nodal point on the half‐space mesh. A load defined here is projected onto adjacent QUAD elements at that node.  
     – Special test mode: If NO = 0, the system interprets this as an instruction to distribute a uniform, constant load across every QUAD element in the half‐space. This shortcut is intended for quick verification and sensitivity studies.  
   • Unit: “—” (no physical units; it is purely an integer index)  
   • Default: “!” (must be explicitly provided; there is no implicit default)

2. Item: PZ  
   • Description: Magnitude of the applied load in the global Z direction (typically vertical).  
     – Positive values of PZ denote downward (compressive) loads.  
     – Negative values, if permitted, would represent uplift or tension, but within the half‐space settlement calculation, only untensioned (compression) effects are normally considered.  
   • Unit: kN (kilonewtons)  
   • Default: 0 (if omitted, no vertical load is applied at the specified node or, in the special case NO=0, across all elements)

Contextual Notes on Workflow and Use Cases:  
• Load‐Case Management: Before invoking a settlement analysis, the user must create or select a load case identifier via an “LC” command (for example, “LC 101”).  
• Executing a Load Record: Once the load case is active, issuing the command “LOAD NO <node> PZ <value>” initiates a fresh settlement solution for that LC. All previous settlement loads under the same LC are discarded.  
• Stiffness Consideration: The procedure deliberately omits any structural or FE-derived stiffness matrices. It assumes the half-space behaves as an elastic, homogeneous medium and calculates settlement purely under the specified vertical loads.  
• Special Verification Mode: Setting NO = 0 (e.g. “LC 101; LOAD NO 0 PZ 1.0”) applies 1 kN of downward pressure per node across all QUAD faces. This is a convenient way to check the model’s baseline response without individually targeting nodes.  
• Best Practices:  
   – Always pair each “LOAD” record with a preceding “LC” statement to ensure clarity and reproducibility.  
   – When redefining loads for an existing LC, expect a full re-analysis rather than incremental superposition.  
   – Use the NO=0 option sparingly for debugging; real case studies should target physically meaningful node sets.

By following these conventions, users can perform rapid, isolated settlement calculations on a half-space mesh, free from the complexity of full FE coupling, while maintaining precise control over node‐based load application.

See also: HALF, LC
 LOAD
 For an input of loads with LOAD a separate settlement calculation is executed (see record LC). The loads are interpreted as untensioned loads on the halfspace. The stiffnesses from a FE system are not considered. If a load case with the same number already exists, it will be deleted.
 One separate settlement analysis that can be used for test purposes is specifying the node number 0, which causes a constant load to be applied [e.g.: LC 101 ; LOAD NO 0 PZ 1.0] at all halfspace QUAD elements.

The table in question defines two optional input parameters—NO and ZR—used to control the generation of stress output at specified nodes and depths in a layered half-space analysis. It is laid out in four columns (Item, Description, Unit, Default) and two rows (one per parameter). Below is a structured, detailed breakdown suitable for ingestion into a RAG/vector store:

1. Table Structure  
   • Columns  
     – Item: Parameter name.  
     – Description: Textual explanation, including how the parameter influences results.  
     – Unit: Physical units (if any) expected for the parameter value.  
     – Default: Value assumed when the parameter is omitted.  
   • Rows  
     – NO: Node number selector  
     – ZR: Depth-of-interest selector  

2. Parameter “NO” (Node Number)  
   • Purpose  
     – Identifies a specific node in the finite-element mesh (or discretized geometry) at which stress outputs are requested. If omitted, the software does not restrict output to a single location; instead it computes Z coordinates for every node in the model.  
   • Description Details  
     – “Node number.”  
     – “If NO is not specified, Z coordinates are calculated for all points.”  
   • Unit  
     – Unitary (no physical unit – represented by a dash).  
   • Default Behavior  
     – With no explicit NO value, stresses are extracted (and full Z coordinate computation is performed) for every node on all layer boundaries.  

3. Parameter “ZR” (Depth to be Examined)  
   • Purpose  
     – Specifies a positive depth value relative to the half-space surface at which the stress state should be evaluated. Acts as a planar cross-section through layered materials.  
   • Description Details  
     – “Depth to be examined (relative to halfspace surface, to be input always positive, independent if global Z goes up or down).”  
     – Notes that in legacy versions, a parameter named Z had the same role.  
   • Unit  
     – Meters (m)  
   • Default Value  
     – 0 (i.e., stresses at the surface of the half-space)  

4. Contextual Notes & Cross-References  
   • “See also: SELP, SELE”  
     – Indicates related commands or parameters elsewhere in the documentation that may adjust element selection (SELE) or point/element print options (SELP).  
   • Stress Output Behavior  
     – The additional remark (“Without an input of a depth Z, stresses are output for node NO at all layer boundaries.”) ties together NO and ZR: if ZR is omitted while NO is provided, stress results will be computed at every material interface for the specified node. Conversely, if both are omitted, the software defaults to full-field stress and coordinate output for all nodes.  

5. Typical Usage Scenarios  
   • Single-node, single-depth query:  
     SET STRESS, NO=15, ZR=2.0  
     → Computes stresses at node 15, 2 m below the surface.  
   • Node-only query:  
     SET STRESS, NO=15  
     → Returns stress values at node 15 across all layer boundaries.  
   • Full-field surface query:  
     SET STRESS  
     → Retrieves Z coordinates and stresses for every node at z = 0 (default depth).  

By capturing parameter names, expected units, defaults, and interplay between NO and ZR, this description provides a clear, self-contained reference entry geared toward precise retrieval in retrieval-augmented generation or vectorized documentation systems.

See also: SELP
 SELE
 Without an input of a depth Z, stresses are output for node NO at all layer boundaries.

The table defines the six keywords (items) available under the SELP input record and documents, for each, the meaning, expected unit, and default‐value behavior. Together, they control how bedding stresses (from half‐space analyses) are stored, optionally extruded into brick (“BRIC”) elements or regular grids, and assigned to load‐case numbers. Below is a detailed breakdown:

1. ZR  
   • Description: Depth at which stresses will be sampled and stored (measured downward from the half‐space surface). Only nonnegative values (≥ 0.0) are accepted.  
   • Unit: none (just a length relative datum; internally meters).  
   • Default: “–” (if omitted but accompanied by multiple LCST values, SELP will cycle through depths and auto‐increment load‐case numbers; if omitted altogether, no stress storage in depth is triggered).

2. LCST  
   • Description: Integer index under which the computed stresses are recorded (“load‐case storage number”). In subsequent WING (post‐processing) runs you refer to this index to plot contours (e.g. CONT P with LC = 101).  
   • Unit: none.  
   • Default: “!” (mandatory unless a default set elsewhere; must be specified for SELP to know where to write).

3. BRIC  
   • Description: Path/filename (32‐character literal, LIT32) for a new database (.cdb) that will receive brick elements, each carrying nodal stress results. Brick elements are generated by extruding the QUAD interface elements.  
   • Unit: LIT32 (string).  
   • Default: “*” (optional; if provided, an auxiliary .cdb is created in addition to the primary LCST‐based results).

4. DX  
   • Description: Grid offset in the global X‐direction. When used with BRIC, DY and HMIN, the half‐space interface’s bounding box is expanded by ±DX prior to meshing.  
   • Unit: meters.  
   • Default: “!” (required if you intend to produce a regularly spaced BRIC‐GRID output).

5. DY  
   • Description: Grid offset in the global Y‐direction. Analogous to DX, it expands the footprint in the Y‐axis.  
   • Unit: meters.  
   • Default: “!” (required for full BRIC‐GRID specification).

6. HMIN  
   • Description: Minimum allowed grid‐cell size when laying out a regular surface mesh (to be extruded into bricks). Controls mesh refinement at the interface.  
   • Unit: meters.  
   • Default: “!” (needed when generating a structured BRIC‐GRID output).

Additional remarks on behavior:  
• Single LCST without accompanying depths causes SELP to interpret successive ZR values as a sequence of depths, automatically incrementing LCST for each. Thus, one run may yield n_depth × n_LC stored cases.  
• If BRIC is specified without DX/DY/HMIN, only the elements directly under the interface (extruded QUADs) are output. Adding DX, DY, HMIN invokes the GRID generator (section 3.3):  
   1) find and expand the bounding box of interface QUADs by DX/DY  
   2) create a 2D grid at surface with spacing no larger than HMIN  
   3) extrude that mesh vertically to form 3D bricks carrying stress and settlement results.  
• File‐name for BRIC may be supplied on a separate line (no ZR needed then).  
• This flexible scheme lets users extract stresses at arbitrary planes (depths), archive them by load case, and either post‐process via contour plots or build full 3D brick stress/settlement models for further analyses or visualization.

Both panels use similar color shading (pale to deeper blues and hints of green) to indicate element identity and stress distribution.

Panel a) “Original system”

Panel b) “Newly generated database containing stresses at the nodes of the BRIC elements”  
• Two extruded, column-shaped blocks correspond to the meshes in panel a: the taller, larger-footprint block is F1; the narrower, slightly shorter block is F2.  
• Each block is built from stacked brick elements (BRIC), formed by extruding the original 2×2 surface mesh vertically through multiple layers. The F1 column shows three vertical layers, producing a 2×2×3 mesh of bricks; F2 shows four or five vertical layers, yielding a 2×2×4 (or 5) arrangement.

This table defines the syntax and semantics of the ECHO record used to control which results are written out by the analysis program.  The ECHO record consists of two fields—OPT and VAL—each of which is described below, together with their allowed values, units and defaults.  In order to be recognized in the input deck, any use of these arguments must be preceded by the literal “ECHO”.

1.  Field: OPT  
    •  Type: literal (LIT)  
    •  Purpose: selects which categories of data are to be output  
    •  Allowed values (each one is a case-sensitive keyword):  
       – PROF   → soil profile values  
       – PILE   → pile‐element data  
       – NODE   → nodal values, load radii  
       – ELEM   → element‐wise results  
       – STRE   → stresses  
       – DISP   → displacements  
       – HALF   → half‐space characteristic values  
       – NPRO   → profile values at nodes  
       – LOAD   → applied loads  
       – BEDD   → foundation (bedding) stresses  
       – STAT   → statistics and CPU timing summaries  
       – FULL   → shorthand for “turn on all options”  
    •  Units: not applicable (LIT)  
    •  Default behavior (when OPT is omitted or set to FULL):  
       – PROF, NODE, ELEM, and LOAD default to NO output  
       – all other options default to YES (i.e. their output is enabled)  

    Note:  You may disable storage of bedding stresses explicitly with “ECHO BEDD OFF”.  For debugging purposes, “ECHO BEDD 77” will cause the program to record the equivalent bedding modulus (computed as bedding stress divided by deformation), but the plot title in the graphical post-processor (WINGRAF) will be labeled incorrectly.

2.  Field: VAL  
    •  Type: either a literal (LIT) or the special flag “–” (dash)  
    •  Purpose: specifies the level of output requested for the chosen OPT category  
    •  Allowed values:  
       – OFF    → no calculation and no output for the specified OPT  
       – NO     → suppress output (but calculations may still occur internally)  
       – YES    → produce standard (regular) output  
       – FULL   → produce extensive output for deeper diagnostics  
       – EXTR   → produce the maximum (“full output”) detail available  
    •  Units: none (–/LIT)  
    •  Default: FULL  

Usage summary:  
When the ECHO record is processed, the program reads the OPT keyword to determine which result sets the user is interested in seeing.  It then applies the VAL parameter to each selected OPT to determine whether that data should be: completely omitted (OFF), computed but not printed (NO), printed in normal form (YES), printed in extended form (FULL), or printed in extra-verbose form (EXTR).  If OPT is set to FULL, all categories defined under the OPT list become active, with their individual defaults or overridden VAL settings taking effect.

ECHO
 EXTR Full output
 The default is NO for PROF, NODE, ELEM and LOAD, and YES for all others.
 The storage of the bedding stresses can be switched off with ECHO BEDD OFF. For test pur- poses, ECHO BEDD 77 causes the equivalent bedding modulus (beddingstress/deformation) to be stored as bedding - but then the title in the WINGRAF plot is wrong.
 This record must be preceded by its name ECHO to avoid confusion with similarly- named record arguments.

The profiles are output only if modifications occurred or output is requested with ECHO PROF. The table is identical to that of the program AQUA.
 The table of the bore profiles used in the calculation is also printed. The bore profiles selected with the record BORE appear here.

Below is a structured, detailed description of the halfspace‐definition table and its fields.  This write-up explains what each column and row means, where its values originate, and how it would typically be used in a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) vector store context.

1. Context  
  • This table is produced by default for every “halfspace” definition in the AQUA program.  
  • It can be suppressed by the directive “ECHO HALF NO.”  
  • Each row or column entry corresponds to a specific record, parameter, or computed metric that governs how contact loads, stiffness, and influence radii are handled on that halfspace.

2. Column‐level entries  
  a. soil profile  
     – Identifier of the soil profile (integer).  
     – Sourced from the PROF record in the input deck.  
  b. HALF (number of layers)  
     – Total number of sublayers assigned to this halfspace.  
     – Read from BLAY (AQUA) layering information.  
  c. top-halfspace [m]  
     – Global Z–coordinate of the top boundary of the halfspace (in meters).  
     – Defines the elevation at which contact computations begin.  
  d. min-load-radius [m]  
     – Minimum radius within which loads are applied, in meters.  
     – Taken directly from the LOAR record.  
  e. beam-load-radius [m]  
     – Default “influence radius” assigned to beam nodes (in meters).  
     – Used to limit how far a beam’s stiffness contributes to the global matrix, thereby reducing bandwidth.  
  f. influence-radius [m]  
     – Alias for beam-load-radius; helps control matrix sparsity in contact regions.  
  g. direction of bedding (Factor: X, Y, Z)  
     – Three numbers summing to 100% that distribute total bedding stiffness along global X, Y, and Z axes.  
     – Allows anisotropic stiffness modeling per halfspace.

3. Row-level or computed quantities  
  a. contact area [m²]  
     – Sum of all nodal contact patch areas on the halfspace surface.  
     – Useful for normalizing pressure or evaluating contact coverage.  
  b. total number nodes  
     – Count of nodes eligible to make contact at that halfspace’s top surface.  
  c. active quad nodes  
     – Number of QUAD (four‐node surface) nodes actually found on the upper boundary.  
     – These nodes receive quadrilateral element contributions for load distribution.  
  d. active quad elements  
     – Count of QUAD shell/surface elements on the top halfspace.  
     – Employed when computing load-radius adjustments or patch integration.  
  e. active quad area [m²]  
     – Total physical area covered by the active QUAD elements.  
  f. beam nodes  
     – Number of nodes in this halfspace not connected to any QUAD element (i.e., beam‐only nodes).  
  g. Maximum bedding stress for non-linear analysis  
     – The upper stress limit defined in the PLAS record, in kN/m².  
     – Governs yield or softening behavior in non-linear bedding models.

4. Usage in RAG vector store  
  • Each field can be tokenized as a “feature” for embeddings (e.g. {“soil_profile”:3}, {“beam_load_radius”:0.5}).  
  • The units and source records (PROF, LOAR, PLAS) should be stored alongside values as metadata.  
  • Queries such as “Which halfspace has the smallest beam_load_radius?” or “List halfspaces where X-direction bedding > 50%” can be answered by filtering this structured table.

Line thickness is constant throughout, emphasizing geometry rather than stress or moment magnitudes by color.  The deflected shape has a continuous, smoothly varying surface, implying that the computational model incorporated a distributed soil‐spring (half‐space stiffness or Winkler) foundation, rather than a rigidly supported slab.  

Beneath the wireframe, the caption reads “Figure 5.2: Displaced structure,” indicating that this is the post‐processing visualization of plate deformations from the ASE (Advanced Structural Engineering) program.  The upward displacement shown corresponds to soil reaction and plate bending caused by untensioned wall loads applied along the plate perimeter.  The uniform green grid and absence of shading or contour bands suggest that this is purely a kinematic deformation plot, not a stress contour map. The image is a plan-view plot of the finite-element bending-moment results for a rectangular base plate (6 m × 10 m, thickness 0.30 m) loaded only by the vertical wall pressures. It is presented as Figure 5.3: “Bending moments.”

Overall composition  
• A thin green outline traces the plate boundary (length ≈10 m horizontally, width ≈6 m vertically). No axes ticks or numeric labels are shown, but the green rectangle represents the plan dimensions of the slab.  
• Inside the boundary is an evenly spaced grid of red “cross” symbols at each finite-element node or integration point. These symbols form roughly 8 columns by 12 rows (exact counts vary slightly around the edges) and are laid out on a regularly spaced rectangular mesh.  

Red cross symbols (moment glyphs)  
• Each red symbol is composed of two thin line segments intersecting at their midpoints, making a “plus” or slightly rotated “×” shape.  
• The orientation of these two segments at each node corresponds to the directions of the principal bending-moment axes (major and minor principal moments).  
• The length of each arm of the cross is proportional to the magnitude of the bending moment in that principal direction. Longer arms imply larger moment magnitudes; shorter arms correspond to smaller bending moments.  
• In this plot, the largest crosses (longest arm lengths) are located along the shorter (6 m) edges of the plate—reflecting the negative bending moments induced by the wall line‐loads. In the interior, the crosses shrink in size, indicating lower bending moments toward mid-span.  
• The rotation of the cross arms also changes slightly from node to node, showing how the orientation of the principal moment axes varies across the plate under the applied line loads.  

Mesh and boundary effects  
• A finer concentration of nodes appears near the plate edges, capturing the high gradients of bending moment under the concentrated wall pressures.  
• Toward the center of the plate, the crosses are more uniform in size and orientation, reflecting a smoother moment field in regions of lower loading influence.  

Caption and interpretation  
• The figure is captioned “Figure 5.3: Bending moments,” indicating that this visualization is the output from the ASE program, load case 1, which omitted the self‐weight of the slab (to isolate the negative moments from the wall loads).  
• This moment field would typically be used to identify critical sections for reinforcement design along plate edges and to compare with simpler Winkler‐foundation results (where the edge moments and soil pressures differ).  

In summary, this image provides a clear, quantitative depiction of bending moments in the base plate under pure wall loading, using red moment‐glyph crosses on a green‐outlined plate to convey both magnitude and directional information at each finite‐element node.

The image is a schematic, false‐colour plot of the computed bedding stresses beneath a rectangular base plate, obtained by the stiffness‐coefficient (half‐space) method for load case 1.  Key visual and semantic features are as follows:

1. Overall layout  
   • A thin green line traces the outline of the plate footprint, forming a simple rectangle on an otherwise blank (white) background.  
   • Inside this green frame is an evenly spaced rectangular grid of red numerical labels.  These correspond to the nodal pressures (bedding stresses) in kN/m², exported from the HASE half‐space analysis.  

2. Grid geometry  
   • The nodes are arranged in a regular lattice—eight (8) columns by six (6) rows (for example)—though the exact count may vary slightly depending on cropping.  
   • Horizontal and vertical spacings between labels are uniform, reflecting the discretization of the 6 m × 10 m base plate into a mesh of quadrilateral elements.  

3. Colour and typography  
   • All stress values are printed in a vivid red sans‐serif font, sized to be legible but not overlapping.  
   • The green outline serves purely as a guide to the plate boundary and does not carry data itself.  

4. Numeric stress distribution  
   • Corner and edge nodes show the highest magnitudes (most negative in sign convention), typically around –14 kN/m² on the corners, tapering inward to roughly –12 kN/m² at edge-adjacent points.  
   • Central nodes settle to values closer to –9 … –10 kN/m², forming a relatively flat “plateau” of lower absolute stress in the mid-span.  
   • All values are negative, indicating downward (compressive) bedding loads under the sign convention used by the software.  

5. Caption and figure labelling  
   • Directly beneath the drawing, a simple caption identifies it as “Figure 5.4: Bedding stresses load case 1 – stiffness coefficient method.”  
   • No axes, scales or coordinate ticks are shown; the user must infer physical coordinates from the plate outline and the context in the surrounding text.  

6. Contextual significance  
   • This visualization contrasts with a Winkler‐type model (constant k) by showing a smoother, more realistic stress “footprint” produced by the half‐space stiffness‐coefficient approach.  
   • The pronounced peaks at the plate edges highlight the negative bending moments induced by vertical wall loads, which would be underpredicted (or misplaced) by a uniform‐spring model.  

In summary, the figure provides a clear, node-by-node map of computed bedding pressures for a 6 × 10 m concrete plate (30 cm thick), showing higher stresses around the periphery and more moderate values toward the center—exactly the pattern one expects when the base plate is loaded by untensioned wall loads and the subgrade is modeled as an elastic half‐space.

The image presents a three-dimensional, wire-frame representation of an idealized building‐soil interaction model. Rendered in a uniformly bright green “hidden-line” style, it shows beams, columns, floor slabs and the underlying bottom plate—the latter depicted as a regular mesh of quadrilateral elements lying at global Z = +2.00 m.

Overall Geometry  
• The building frame comprises a grid of vertical columns and horizontal beam elements spanning in orthogonal directions. Three main column lines run in one direction and, in plan, three bays in the perpendicular direction produce a roughly rectangular footprint.  
• Four above-ground storeys are visible—three full storeys with identical slab layouts plus a partial top storey at one end. Each floor slab is represented by QUAD elements that rest on the beam grid.  
• The floor slabs are flat, planar plates of uniform thickness (not explicitly shown) and are meshed densely with quadrilaterals. These slabs receive uniformly distributed loads in the analysis but, since only the bottom plate at Z = 2.00 m is used by the half-space routine, the upper-floor slab elements are excluded from HASE calculations.

Bottom Plate and Foundation Nodes  
• At the base of the model, a regular grid mesh of QUAD elements (192 elements in the HASE input) forms the bottom plate. This plate represents the soil–structure contact surface.  
• Two of the mesh nodes, identified as special “beam nodes” (nodes 1402 and 1406), carry separate spread foundations. Around each of these nodes, a circular influence area of radius 0.70 m is applied to represent an isolated footing.  
• The total loaded contact area (mesh + isolated footings) is approximately 303 m². Horizontal and vertical stiffnesses of the underlying soil half-space are stored at every bottom-plate node, obviating the need for prescribed horizontal fixities.

Structural Members  
• Beams: Shown as straight lines connecting column nodes, forming the primary horizontal load paths. They define each floor outline and interior supports.  
• Columns: Vertical line elements that carry slab and beam loads down to the bottom plate. They are arranged at each beam intersection.  
• Slabs: Horizontally oriented meshes of QUAD elements rest atop the beams at each floor level. Although these are drawn in the same green wire frame, only the lowest plate interacts directly with the soil in the half-space model.

Visualization Style  
• The model uses a hidden-line algorithm (e.g., Program WING with VISI HIDD LINE) to produce a clean, plastic-like appearance, with all lines rendered in a single color for clarity.  
• Omitted are surface fills or shading; instead, the transparency of the wire frame allows simultaneous viewing of internal geometry and spatial relationships between components.

Function in Analysis  
This visual corresponds to the input for a combined frame‐soil analysis:  
• QUAD mesh for soil contact and footing distribution (HASE).  
• Beam & column framework for global stiffness (ASE).  
• Slab QUAD elements for load application on upper storeys (SOFILOAD).  

Together, these elements define a coupled system in which the bottom plate transfers vertical and horizontal reactions into a two-layer soil half-space with stiffness moduli of 90 MPa and 30 MPa, respectively.

Given a building which is idealized as a framework. The bottom plate lies on the ground, which is characterized by two soil layers each having a constant stiffness module. The soil parameters are constant over the plan view. Example - hase2_3d.dat
 The framework is composed of beams elements, and the bottom plate is entered as QUAD elements. Separate foundations are given at the nodes 1402 and 1406. Floor slabs are defined using QUAD elements to complete the load description and to represent the upper floor levels. (In this way the hidden line algorithm supplies more plastic pictures.)
 No fixities are specified in the input. The bottom plate lies at the level z = +2.00m (global Z coordinate).
 The soil profile is defined with the records BORE and BLAY and assigned soil profile number 3 (program AQUA). In the first layer from z = 2.00m to 4.80m, the stiffness modulus is set to 90Mp, and in the second layer only 30Mp. Beneath the global Z coordinate of 9.80m, it is assumed the ground is perfectly rigid. This ends the description of the soil profile.
 +PROG AQUA
 HEAD !... BORE 3 BLAY 2.00 ES 90000 BLAY 4.80 ES 30000 BLAY 9.80 ES 30000 !... END

 HEAD FORMATION OF THE HALFSPACE STIFFNESS MATRIX HALF TYPE CONS PROF 3 Z 2.00 FAKX 1 FAKY 1 FAKZ 1 LOAR BEAM 0.70
 END
 The stiffness is stored in all three directions with FAKX 1 1 1. This precludes the necessity to later specify horizontal fixings. The horizontal loads are distributed over the bottom plate and thereby transferred to the building ground.

The figure presents a plan‐view schematic of a circular gas‐tank foundation discretized into a quadrilateral finite‐element mesh for soil–structure interaction analysis. Drawn in bright green lines on a white background, the mesh consists of an inner, nearly square core of 36 quadrilaterals (6×6 grid) and five concentric rings of progressively curved quadrilaterals that approximate the circular perimeter (nominal radius 11.50 m). Mesh nodes appear at every element corner and mid‐side; a subset of these is highlighted in purple, indicating boundary‐condition or support‐stiffness nodes where horizontal stiffness is set at 50 % of the vertical stiffness.

Seven borehole test locations are overlaid as small white circles with black numerals (4, 7, 11, 12, 13, 15, 22). These correspond exactly to the input coordinates in the AQUA and SOFIMSHA programs and feed into HASE for half‐space stiffness interpolation. Bore 4 sits at the geometric center (X=0 m, Y=0 m). Bore 7 lies on the east radial axis at (9 m, 0 m). Bore 11 is plotted northeast at roughly (9 m, 8 m), while Bore 12 appears north‐northwest at (–1 m, 6 m). Bore 13 is west‐northwest at (–5 m, 7 m); Bore 15 is southwest at (–9 m, –1 m); and Bore 22 is south at (1 m, –9 m). These points form an irregular ring around the center, enabling coordinate‐based interpolation of soil layers (BLAY depths) and elastic moduli (ES values) in program SOFIMSHA.

The mesh connectivity data (169 top‐half‐space nodes, 156 active elements) and control parameters (influence radius = 4 m, weight exponent EP = 2) ensure that each bore profile exerts a stiffness influence proportional to the inverse square of its distance. This produces a spatially varying half‐space stiffness matrix with a bandwidth limited to nodes within 4 m of a given bore. The polygonal QUAD discretization yields a contact area of 410.746 m², very close to the analytical circle area (π·11.5² ≈ 415.5 m²). This plan, labeled “Figure 5.10: Bore locations in the plan,” underpins the subsequent ASE structural analysis, which computes differential settlements, tank inclination due to plan‐view soil variability, and nonuniform normal stresses across radial quadrilaterals.

The image presents a three-dimensional wire-frame rendering—shown entirely in bright green—of a cylindrical storage tank (bottom plate, shell and roof) after elastic settlement of its foundation has been computed and magnified five hundred times. A brief breakdown of what the viewer sees:

Overall Geometry and Mesh  
• Bottom Plate: A roughly circular, flat disc (radius ≈11.5 m), discretized by quadrilateral shell elements. The mesh lines form concentric rings and radial “spokes,” mapping the plate’s geometry.  
• Cylindrical Shell: Rising from the plate’s outer rim, a short cylindrical wall carries a conical or domed roof. The shell is likewise meshed with quadrilateral elements in both circumferential and vertical directions.  
• Roof: The top appears as a single apex point with mesh lines radiating downward, suggesting a conical or truncated-dome cap.

Viewpoint and Deformation Pattern  
• Perspective: The model is viewed off-center, slightly above the tank, looking down at an oblique angle. The highest point (roof apex) appears at the top of the frame, while the foreground shows the plate’s front edge dipping downward.  
• Settlement Signal: One side of the base plate is clearly displaced downward more than the opposite side—evidence of non-uniform soil stiffness in plan. The grid on the plate bows and twists, indicating bending of the plate under differential settlement.  
• Tilt: The entire shell and roof assembly leans gently in the same direction as the plate’s surface, revealing how the structure inclines due to variable subgrade conditions.

Analysis Context (from accompanying text)  
• Interpolation Scheme: Soil‐profile parameters were interpolated in plan between eight borehole locations using a distance‐squared weighting (influence exponent EP = 2) and a 4 m radius of influence.  
• Halfspace Model: A boundary‐element halfspace stiffness matrix was assembled (horizontal stiffness set to 50% of vertical). The bottom plate’s mesh area (≈410.7 m²) closely matches its circular area (r=11.5 m) accounting for polygonal discretization.  
• Condensed Diagram: Deformations are multiplied by a “condensed diagram factor” of 500 to make small actual settlements visible.

Caption and Notation  
• At bottom of image reads: “Figure 5.11: Deformed structure (condensed diagram factor 500).”  
• All mesh lines are uniform in thickness and color, emphasizing geometry and deformation pattern rather than color‐coded stress or displacement magnitudes.

In sum, the rendering is a post-processing visualization from a finite‐element/halfspace soil–structure interaction analysis, illustrating how uneven soil properties beneath the tank cause non-uniform settlement and incline the entire structure when magnified for clarity.

The image is a three-dimensional wireframe rendering of a circular, conical-roof storage tank, annotated as “Figure 5.13: Principal normal stress n-I.” The structure sits on a circular base and tapers to a central apex at the top, suggesting either a conical roof on a cylindrical shell or a simplified model of the bottom plate deflected under load (context indicates principal stress contours on the bottom plate of a tank).

Key visual features:

• Overall geometry  
  – A circular plan, shown in perspective, with the major horizontal axis roughly left–right and the minor axis front–back.  
  – The shell side is rendered as a series of radial “spokes” (vertical green lines) emanating from the apex down to the edge of the base.  
  – Concentric horizontal rings (blue, red, and green circuits) slice the shell or plate at discrete elevations; these rings illustrate contours of equal principal stress.

• Mesh and contour lines  
  – Vertical grid (meridian) lines in vivid green divide the circumference into equal angular segments (approximately 24 to 30 radial divisions).  
  – Horizontal contour lines are shown in three colors:  
     • Red: these circles appear at the highest and lowest elevations, marking zones of maximum positive principal stress (n-I).  
     • Blue: the mid-elevation rings are colored in blue, indicating intermediate stress levels.  
     • Green: finer grid lines running over the mesh (both meridional and azimuthal) serve as reference geometry rather than stress contours.

• Stress interpretation  
  – The red rings at bottom and at the very top suggest peak normal stresses around the tank’s base edge and near the apex, respectively.  
  – Blue rings in the mid-section show moderate stress; the spacing between blue and red rings gives a qualitative sense of stress gradation in the radial (and vertical) directions.  
  – The uniformity of the rings around the circumference implies axisymmetric loading, though slight non-uniformity is conceivable given the contour spacing.

• Visual perspective  
  – The viewpoint is elevated and slightly to the front-right, allowing simultaneous view of the tank’s roof apex, mid-section contours, and base edge.  
  – The lower edge of the base plate projects as a faint green polygonal ring, its slight faceting illustrating that the circular base is approximated by QUAD finite elements (text cites “polygonal description” and reported contact area).

• Relation to context  
  – This image aligns with the textual description of a finite-element analysis performed in programs SOFILOAD and ASE: the principal normal stress field (n-I) under combined dead load and tank contents.  
  – The contour colors correspond to stress magnitudes computed at nodes of the halfspace-stiffness model: red for higher stresses near the edge (where settlement differences and support stiffness transitions occur), blue for intermediate values at mid-radii.  
  – The mesh density (meridians and parallels) reflects the model’s nodal setup: 169 active nodes in the top halfspace, as noted in the HASE output.

In sum, the figure provides a clear, color-coded depiction of the first principal normal stress distribution on a circular tank foundation or shell. The red, blue, and green wireframe conveys both the geometric discretization (finite-element mesh) and the resulting stress contour levels, offering an immediate visual of where stresses concentrate under the applied loading and soil interaction conditions.

The image is a plan‐view schematic of the circular bottom plate of a storage tank, annotated as “Figure 5.12: Displacements u-z of the bottom plate.”  It presents the calculated vertical settlement (u-z) of the plate as a series of contour lines, showing how the plate has deformed under combined dead load and tank contents.  Key visual elements are:  

• Outer boundary: drawn in green, this approximate circle represents the plate’s edge, which in the finite‐element model is actually a polygonal ring of quadrilateral elements.  Its nominal radius is 11.5 m.  
• Contour lines: in blue, a set of roughly concentric closed curves indicates loci of equal vertical deflection.  There are about ten contours, each nested inside the next, with the smallest loop around the zone of maximum settlement.  The spacing between contours is uniform in terms of deflection increment, illustrating the gradient of settlement from the edge toward the most compressed region.  
• Node markers: small magenta symbols (dots or short crosses) are placed around the outer boundary at the modeled node points (where the halfspace and plate stiffness interact).  They emphasize the finite‐element discretization and the locations at which soil parameters were interpolated.  
• Asymmetry of contours: the center of the contour pattern is visibly shifted to the right of the plate’s geometric center.  This indicates that the tank has tilted slightly in plan, due to variations in the subsoil stiffness and layer depths around its circumference.  The side showing denser, more closely spaced contours corresponds to stiffer or shallower soil, which restricts settlement; the side with wider spacing is softer or deeper, allowing greater deflection.  
• Absence of color shading: rather than a filled contour map, this plot relies purely on linework to display u-z.  In a RAG (retrieval augmented generation) or vector‐store context, each contour line could be tagged with its numerical deflection value (not shown in the graphic) and indexed by location.  

Overall, the graphic conveys how the bottom plate deforms nonuniformly under load, directly reflecting the coordinate‐interpolated soil profile around the borehole sample points and the influence‐factor weighting (EP = 2, radius = 4 m) used in the halfspace stiffness assembly.  The visualization supports interpretation of settlement, tilt, and load distribution prior to stress analysis in program ASE.

The image presents a three-dimensional wireframe rendering of a rectangular soil half-space discretized with hexahedral finite elements, onto which a rigid bottom plate has been placed. The entire model is shown in blue lines against a white background, emphasizing the geometry and mesh layout rather than material shading or color contours. Key features and observations include:

1. Overall Geometry  
   • The half-space is modeled as a large rectangular block, its top surface originally flat but now deformed under load.  
   • The bottom plate is represented as a slightly thinner, planar polygon embedded flush with the top surface prior to deformation; in the deformed view it leaves a clear imprint in the mesh above it.

2. Mesh Discretization  
   • The central region directly beneath and immediately around the plate contains relatively small, regular brick elements—squares in plan view—providing high resolution where stress and settlement gradients are greatest.  
   • A narrow ring of very thin, flattened elements surrounds the plate at a uniform gap of approximately 10 cm. This gap separates the plate nodes (loaded) from the surrounding soil nodes (initially unloaded), allowing distinct boundary conditions.  
   • Beyond this thin ring, elements increase progressively in size and aspect ratio—the outer shell of very large hexahedra—minimizing total element count and CPU time without compromising the overall representation of far-field behavior.

3. Surface Deformation and Impression  
   • The deformed mesh surface clearly shows a “bowl-shaped” settlement pattern, with maximum vertical displacement directly above the plate footprint and diminishing smoothly into the surrounding soil.  
   • The impression of the rigid plate is seen as a flattened plateau at the center of the depression, reflecting the constraint that plate nodes cannot move relative to one another.  
   • Mesh lines curve smoothly from the undeformed far field toward the deformation trough, illustrating the half-space’s elastic response under the plate load.

4. Context of Analysis  
   • Although no stress contours or numeric values are overlaid in this particular figure, the geometry and refinement pattern signal an earlier or subsequent computation of vertical stresses and settlements (e.g., for depths of 1 m, 2 m, … up to 20 m).  
   • In full workflow, stresses at specified depths would be stored in separate load cases, and contour plotting (as done later in WING) would reveal concentrations—especially beneath pile footings—at selected depths such as 10 m.

Together, these details make the image a clear demonstration of how a bottom‐plate load is transferred into a discretized half-space, how mesh grading facilitates accurate capture of deformation around critical areas, and how boundary definitions (gaps and zero‐stiffness display elements) allow separate visualization of plate and soil response.

The image is a two-dimensional cut-through (plan/arbitrary section) of a half-space finite-element model at a constant depth Z = 5 m, showing the distribution of vertical stresses under a stiff bottom plate and into the surrounding soil. It was generated by the WING post-processor reading stress load cases from a HASE run (in this case LC 105 for Z = 5 m).

1. Overall Layout  
• A large rectangular boundary in bright green delineates the outer “display” region of the half-space mesh. This boundary is not load-bearing (GRP…STI 0 elements) but simply represents the extent of discretization.  
• Centered within that, a stepped, cross-shaped polygon in the same bright green color marks the footprint of the stiff bottom plate (“bottom slab”) which transfers the column loads to the piles and into the soil.  
• Two orthogonal blue lines—horizontal and vertical—cross at the geometric center of the bottom plate. These are the reference axes along which stress values have been extracted and plotted.

2. Stress Plotting  
• Along both the horizontal axis (left-to-right) and the vertical axis (top-to-bottom), a red line traces the computed vertical normal stress σz at Z = 5 m. The line sweeps across the entire domain, rising and falling in response to plate edges and pile locations.  
• At regular intervals along each axis, red numeric labels indicate stress magnitude (units consistent with the input data, e.g. kN/m²). Peaks coincide with the edges and corners of the stiff plate footprint, illustrating stress concentrations. Between these peaks, the curve dips as the stress vault spreads out.

3. Finite-Element Discretization Features  
• Immediately adjacent to the green plate polygon, the mesh employs a ring of very thin elements (not directly visible but implied by the sharp curvature of the stress contours) to capture the high curvature of the soil surface imprint.  
• A narrow 10 cm gap was introduced between the plate edge nodes and the first ring of surrounding nodes; this allows the software to assign zero stiffness to the outer “display only” elements while preserving full stiffness for the plate.  
• Radiating outward beyond the thin-element ring, element size increases markedly—reflected in the straight green boundary—so as to minimize the total element count and CPU time without affecting the stress field near the plate.

4. Interpretation

Key Observations
